003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.name: Five textile fragments.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.description:
Five circular woollen textile fragments each decorated with a depiction of a bird, perhaps a duck or a goose, in different sizes and colours, and woven in a non-extended weft pattern, a tapestry technique. The fragments were taken from bigger textiles, perhaps used as a counterpane or curtains, and which may have consisted of a decorative design with repetitive motifs. Upper Egypt was famous for sumptuous woven cloth such as this, with Asyut, Akhmim and the City of Fustat prominent places of production during the Tulunid period (AH 3rd / AD 9th century).  
During the Tulunid period, textiles were distinguished by the appearance of a shadow in the decorative components, where the colour was graded from light to dark, as well as for their powerful expression. They were also influenced by the Sassanid style, brought by Ahmad ibn Tulun (r. AH 254–70 / AD 868–84) from Iraq. The production of textiles in the Tulunid period represents a period of transition in Egypt between the Coptic period and the Islamic period with regard to the decorative components and their development.  
Most of the *jizya* (tribute) which Ahmad ibn Tulun sent to the court of the Abbasid caliphs consisted of textiles made in the *Tiraz* workshops, under royal decree, which produced magnificent fabrics of wool and linen. Tulun took a personal interest in the textile factories of Egypt, which were widespread in the north delta regions of Tanis, Dabik, Damietta, and other cities. These regions were famous for the manufacture of linen cloth with inscriptions woven in silk in a multitude of colours. Interest in textile manufacture increased in Egypt with the rule of the sons of Ibn Tulun: Khumarawayh (r. AH 270–82 / AD 884–96) and Harun (r. AH 283–92 / AD 896–905), who were inclined towards recording their names in inscription bands on the textile itself.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.short_description: Cotton and linen textiles were woven in various factories in Egypt: Alexandria, Damietta, Farma, Bahnasa, Akhmim and Asyut. Coptic-style decorations remained prevalent during the AH 1st–3rd / AD 7th–9th centuries. The pieces here are notable for the shadow effect in the decorations, where colour is graded from light to dark shades.

003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.method_for_datation: These fragments have been dated based on a study of their decorative components that include the depiction of birds similar to those found in Tulunid *Tiraz* textiles from the Upper Egypt region, and which also resemble the depictions of birds on other Iraqi applied arts with Sassanid roots. Furthermore, the colours used in these textiles, whether it be different shades of yellow, degrees of green or blue, are colours that were customary on Tulunid textiles.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.method_for_provenance: Egypt was famed during the Tulunid period for its textile industry where magnificent woollen and linen fabrics were produced. The depiction of birds found on these textile fragments are also similar to those found in Tulunid *Tiraz* textiles from Upper Egypt.

012b5222-da31-50c5-8bfc-eb439eea45d0.name: *Flight of the French army and retreat of the Duke of Alençon across the Ticino*
012b5222-da31-50c5-8bfc-eb439eea45d0.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the right-hand border of the tapestry; the mark can also be found on another example in the series. The presence of the weaver’s mark has also allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here, placed in the sequence suggested by Paredes, constitutes the last in the series and should be read in close continuity with the subject represented in the tapestry that precedes it, *Flight of the besieged and retreat of the Swiss who drown in great numbers in the Ticino*. In particular, from the juxtaposition of the two tapestries, the landscape south of Pavia can be recreated, distinguished by the presence of the small island of Gravellone, separated from the city by the waters of the Ticino. The tapestry represents one of the final moments of the battle, with a portrait of the Duke of Alençon – identified by the writing on the caparison of his horse – who, after having crossed the bridge of boats on the Ticino, orders its destruction to prevent the enemy from following. In the foreground, a few infantrymen are depicted, busy destroying the bridge, while a horseman and other soldiers are the last to cross it. The action of the Duke of Alençon, brother-in-law of the King of France, condemns all those who do not manage to cross the bridge to the wrath of the enemy or to the swirling waters of the river. In the distance, one can glimpse a herd of cows grazing serenely, indifferent to the war, in the rural landscape.

01c1fd3b-239c-5a49-b106-2c0d2c8ff5bf.name: Textile fragment
01c1fd3b-239c-5a49-b106-2c0d2c8ff5bf.description: This fragment of a scene depicting hunters on camels indicates the extraordinary skill of the Safavid weavers. Another fragment of this textile showing six hunters is in the Keir Collection at the Dallas Museum of Art. In the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts' piece, two turbaned riders hunting gazelles with spears stand out against an orangey red background adorned with rocks and plant designs. The subject of the scene – hunting on camelback – is borrowed from a story that the Persian poet Nizami (AD 1141–1209) told about the Sasanian King Bahram Gur (AD 420–438/39). The theme of the royal hunt figured prominently in Achaemenid and Sasanian decorative arts, providing a favourite motif for Safavid weaving and the miniatures of the period.

020537ba-c7e7-5283-b409-13ae6ef0caa1.name: Ikat hanging
020537ba-c7e7-5283-b409-13ae6ef0caa1.short_description:
The decoration of this wall hanging is characteristic of the 19th century: It shows a cypress tree, here flanked by two smaller trees, in a niche. The central motif is bordered on the right and left by a wide border, reminiscent of borders on carpets.  
  
The hanging is made using the ikat technique, yet in this case a far more complex material choice has been employed, not being made simply from silk or cotton but as an ikat velvet. They were made in Kashan, possibly also in Yazd. On the basis of some inscribed objects, a period of manufacture from 1896 to 1925 is attested, i.e. exactly until the end of the Qajar period.

04d27671-b1ac-5ad5-85cb-254ee0e80def.name: Bridal cushion
04d27671-b1ac-5ad5-85cb-254ee0e80def.description: This bridal cushion from Ma’an, Jordan, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, is among the most distinctive examples of Jordanian domestic textiles. They feature embroidery patterns that are believed to reflect connections with the Caucasus, whether through historical travel, trade, or settlement. These motifs stand as a testament to Ma'an's role as a crossroads of cultural exchange, where influences from distant regions were absorbed into local artistic traditions.

05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.name: Silk fragment.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.description: A fragment of linen and silk textile that is tapestry-woven. It has four horizontal silk panels that alternate between areas of woven linen and vertical blue silk stripes. The uppermost band shows a broad, gathered band that is interlaced in gold and outlined in red. The spaces within the interlacing are filled with gold-coloured motifs above and below, and abstract floral motifs rendered in gold and green in the centre; the entirety is flanked above and below by gold-coloured split-palmette scroll borders set against a red background. Below this is a band of cursive Arabic script, rendered in blue and set against a plain background, again flanked by gold-coloured split-palmette scroll borders. The stripe beneath this, which features borders identical to those above, shows an elegant gold-coloured *kufic* inscription, with red detailing, set against a deep-blue background. The final band consists of two superposed strips of gold-coloured split-palmette scrolls with red outlines.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.short_description: Textile fragments with this type of decoration and epigraphic detail are typical of Fatimid Egypt, famous for the production of luxury textiles. Many were found in burials in Upper Egypt. This textile was collected by Henry Wallis (1830–1916), a famous painter and expert on Middle Eastern ceramics.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.dates: Hegira the 540s to 70s / AD second quarter of the 12th century.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.method_for_datation: The style of the inscription encountered on this fragment is closely related to a linen fragment with tapestry-woven silk elements in the Bouvier Collection in Geneva, which has been attributed to Fatimid Egypt during the 540s to 570s / second quarter of the 12th century.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that textile fragments with this type of decoration and epigraphic detail were produced in Fatimid Egypt. This is due to so many having been found in burials and excavations throughout Upper Egypt in particular.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.provenance: From a tomb at al-Drounka, Egypt.
05e7e5aa-01c1-5eb2-8d63-892574f025d5.obtention: This textile together with several other Fatimid textile fragments were acquired by NMS in 1898 from Henry Wallis, a famous Pre-Raphaelite painter, who travelled and painted extensively in Egypt and elsewhere. Subsequently he became a highly respected expert on Egyptian and Persian ceramics.

07cfbb4a-25e5-5ae3-a64e-9de990ccf477.description: This bridal cushion from Ma'an, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, reflects the town’s position as a crossroads of cultural exchange. 0bdd9721-3f27-532b-aa49-d29c2756dbbe.name: *Flight of the besieged and retreat of the Swiss who drown in great numbers in the Ticino*
0bdd9721-3f27-532b-aa49-d29c2756dbbe.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here should be viewed immediately after the tapestry with *The taking of Mirabello Castle*, and it precedes the last in the series, *Flight of the French army and retreat of the Duke of Alençon across the Ticino*. In particular, from the juxtaposition of the three tapestries, one can reconstruct on the left the French encampment, bordered in the foreground by the walls of the Visconti Park and by the defensive system composed of a series of gabions, which one can also distinguish in the distance. On the right, one can recreate the landscape south of Pavia, distinguished by the presence of the small island of Gravellone and by the course of the waters of the Ticino.  
Dominating the tapestry is the depiction of the city of Pavia, bordered by walls, with the Visconti Castle on the left and the Covered Bridge on the right. This is the final phase of the battle: troops commanded by Antonio de Leyva burst out of the city besieged by the imperial troops and attack the French army from behind. In the centre, soldiers and civilians come out of their shelters, trying to flee, while several men, pushed towards the Ticino by the imperial cavalry, drown in the river. In the centre of the tapestry, one of the cavaliers of François de Laval, Count of Montfort, can be identified thanks to the writing embroidered on his horse’s harness.

0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.name: The revenge ground of al-Mukhtar (Persian: *Dar al-entegham-e Mokhtar*)
0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.short_description: The tragic martyrdom of the Prophet’s grandson al-Husayn and his companions at Karbala' near Kufa, where they were massacred by an Umayyad army in 61/680, played an important role in the consolidation of the *Shi'i* ethos; it also led to the formation of radical trends among the *Shi'i*. The earliest of such trends became manifest in the movement of al-Mukhtar, who won control of Kufa in an open revolt in 66/685. Aiming to avenge al-Husayn’s murder, al-Mukhtar launched his own movement and proclaimed Ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Husayn’s half-brother Muhammad, as the *Mahdi*, 'the divinely guided one', the messianic saviour imam and restorer of true Islam who would establish justice on earth and deliver the oppressed from tyranny.

Its exterior is edged in red and covered all over with delicate spiral vines made of white leather and set with dark-blue lamellae (scales); two red medallions are placed among them. The back of the quiver is dark-blue except for a narrow edging and two oval gold medallions. The arrow quiver is identical and complements the bow quiver.

0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.name: *Kiswa* (tomb cover) for the Prophet of God, Ibrahim (Abraham).
0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.description:
There was a tradition in both the Mamluk and the Ottoman periods, for sultans, noble personages of state, as well as the benevolent, to interest themselves in the tombs of the prophets and the devout by offering a *kiswa* (covering for a grave or tomb), and then to renew it each year or whenever necessary. The ritual draping of tombs and shrines were popular celebrations that took place in certain seasons every year. For the most part, this occurred in order to procure the good-will and approval of visitors to the tomb or shrine, and to enhance the popularity of the *kiswa*'s donor among the general public. It was during the Ottoman period in Palestine that there was a huge unparalleled interest in the tombs, shrines and holy places that were scattered throughout the region. This was within the context of the official interest in the Sufi orders, their sheikhs, and the venues where the rituals were practiced. An example of this veneration can be seen in the context of the tombs of the Prophets Moses, Samuel and David, and their wives, in al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil).  
The *kiswa* exhibited here is made from woven green silk. The *kiswa* was produced in order to envelope the tomb completely, leaving only the tombstone visible, upon which was written the name of the deceased: “The Prophet of God, Ibrahim \[Abraham\]”. The *tughra* of the Ottoman sultan, Selim III (r. AH 1203-22/AD 1789-1807) is embroidered on the *Kiswa*, together with inscriptions that read, “This is a protector” and “revered”, in addition to other inscriptions that include religious supplications and Qur'anic verses.  
The official tradition as noted above, to send *kiswa*s to the tombs and shrines of venerated holy men and women, continued in Palestine until the end of the Ottoman period in 1916, when the tradition was officially stopped. At the popular level, however, locals who lived in the environs of these tomb sites and shrines continued preparing *kiswas* but they were no longer splendid, finely made textiles as had been the case during the period of the Ottoman sultans.

123265a3-960f-5c76-9487-14f718823b74.name: *Termeh* panel
123265a3-960f-5c76-9487-14f718823b74.short_description: Very popular both in the Eastern world and in Europe, ‘Kashmir shawls’ (Pers. *termeh*) were produced not only in northern India but also in Iran, mostly in Kerman. *Termeh* panels, embroidered with metal thread (in the *sermeh duzi* technique) and occasionally with pearls, were treasured family possessions handed down from generation to generation. When used as wedding gifts they included inscriptions of good wishes to the bride and groom. This sumptuous *termeh* panel features scrolling vines and grapes embroidered with silver strips on the wool ground decorated with *botehs*. Various alternating metal strips and a profusion of pearls enhance the highly suggestive tactile quality of this exquisite embroidery.

14763417-a183-5949-ac5d-11f296d400e1.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
14763417-a183-5949-ac5d-11f296d400e1.short_description: This hanging of red, yellow-golden and green silk is richly embroidered with silver and silver-gilt inscriptions and designs. Above, a lamp with invocations to Allah as the Opener or Judge (ya Fattah) appears suspended from an arched niche resting on two columns. Its spandrels display two roundels with the Islamic profession of Faith (shahada). Below, a quote from chapter 2 (Al-Baqarah), verse 197 of the Holy Qur’an appears: ‘…and the best provision is Al-Taqwa (piety, righteousness)’. In the lower half of the hanging, four roundels with the names of the rightly-guided caliphs surround the imperial Ottoman emblem or tughra of the sultan Abd al- Hamid II  (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD), who commissioned this curtain.. Hangings like this one may have been intended for the prayer niche of the Prophet’s mosque, as earlier examples of this type often include the inscription ‘this is the mihrab of the Prophet (pbuh)’.

14df710b-1ecd-5f46-9a55-9c8986e98145.name: Fragment of golden lampas with capture scene
14df710b-1ecd-5f46-9a55-9c8986e98145.short_description:
Silk figured fabrics (patterns of which included images of people) were at the peak of the Safavid court fashion. A remarkable example of the type is this fragment of a golden lampas depicting a scene of captivity. One of the most technologically sophisticated and costly fabrics in Iran, the golden lampas provided up to 10 silk threads of different colours in the pattern. The inclusion of threads wrapped in gold or silver foil suggest that the fabric could be produced in *karkhane* – imperial workshops.  
The fragment is one of the two largest pieces among seven dispersed parts of a very costly man’s robe that probably belonged to some member of the Iranian Shah family. The scene featured on the lampas has long aroused great interest among researchers. Around a tree (sycamore or maple), where a large fairy bird is sitting on the branch, rides a horseman leading a prisoner. A little child sits behind the rider. Above the people a rooster flies towards a tree.  
The horseman is depicted in the characteristic Safavid outfit of the AD 16th century: a turban is wound around a tall Taj cap, the number of turban bangs symbolizes 12 righteous Shi‘ite imams.  
The idea to treat the scene as a political manifesto of the victorious campaigns of Shah Tahmasp I to Georgia (1540, 1553) was complemented by alternative *Sufi* interpretation of the subject. The scene of captivity was seen as an allegory of man on his spiritual path to God. Thus the horseman stands for the Teacher who leads the Disciple (captive) through the complex ways of learning towards a divine truth personified by the mythical ancient Iranian bird, Simurg (fairy bird).

167452fd-adc4-5a30-86d3-5bf301e4087f.name: Inscribed textile (*tiraz*)
167452fd-adc4-5a30-86d3-5bf301e4087f.short_description:
This *tiraz* was made for the Fatimid caliph al-‘Aziz (Hegira 365–386 / AD 975–996). It testifies to the tractable nature of Fatimid society. Exceptionally, in addition to supplying the caliph’s titles, it gives the name of his chief minister or vizier Ibn Killis (served Hegira 366–380 / AD 977–90). Killis, who was of Jewish origin, was famous for the financial reforms that helped bring enormous prosperity to Egypt as well as to the vizier. The inscription reads,  
Praise to God, Lord of the Worlds, may God bless Muhammad the Prophet. Assistance from God \[to\] Nizar Abu Mansur, the Imam al-‘Aziz billah, Commander of the faithful, God’s blessing upon him and upon \[his pure ancestors\]. From what was ordered by the respectable vizier Abu‘l-Faraj Ya‘qub ibn Yusuf \[Ibn Killis\], vizier of the Commander of the faithful, to be made in the year \[three hundred\] seventy-one.

198af7b8-d119-53c0-a03b-ca6e94c08acd.name: Stole, mirror dressing (*tenchifa*).
198af7b8-d119-53c0-a03b-ca6e94c08acd.description:
A long stole embroidered on both ends and on part of the sides.  
At the ends, the decoration is divided into two sections that precede a fillet of silk thread spirals and a golden thread braid.  
The first section consists of a frieze of wild roses arranged around a cruciform pistil and stylised serrated horseshoe hyacinths arranged obliquely around the fleurons.  
The second section consists of a bouquet of flowers growing from a thick undulating line in green silk representing foliage from which the stems and stylised flowers emerge. The ovoid medallion with serrated edges that finishes it is reminiscent of the pomegranate. The borders between the two end compositions are decorated with floral motifs suggesting small butterflies and finished with a golden braid.  
All of these motifs would have been embroidered by women with brightly and harmoniously coloured thread. The black silk line that surrounds them enhances the design.  
Stoles of this type were hung around mirror frames during festivals to ward off the evil eye. Although the composition and floral motifs are borrowed from the vegetal embroidery of the Algerian Ottomans, the very free stylisation distances it from this original model and sets the piece apart, constituting a genre in itself.
198af7b8-d119-53c0-a03b-ca6e94c08acd.short_description: This long stole is embroidered on both ends and part of the sides and would have been hung around mirror frames on feast days to ward off the evil eye. Its compositions and floral motifs, although stylised, are borrowed from the plant repertoire of Algerian Ottoman embroidery.

1b9107ef-851d-52ee-bc3e-ab6407fccbb8.name: Sarong
1b9107ef-851d-52ee-bc3e-ab6407fccbb8.short_description:
The harmonious marriage of the iridescent colours in Malay textiles is perhaps best seen in examples of finely woven *kain limar*. The single weft-ikat cloth, also known as *kain lemar* or *kain limau*, is principally produced in the state of Terengganu and Kelantan on the East Coast of the Malay Peninsula. While these cloths are now associated with the Sultanate of Terengganu, in the past they were also part of royal ceremonial costume in the Riau and Lingga archipelago, which lie between the Malay Peninsula and southern Sumatra.

20111b76-70e4-5b40-874b-20a4d142f81d.name: Fragment of woven silk.
20111b76-70e4-5b40-874b-20a4d142f81d.description:
A blue silk woven with a quatrefoil design, bordered by inscriptions, and a polyfoil occupying the spaces in between. The inscription, written in Arabic reads: ‘Honour to al-Ashraf’. The development and chronology of Mamluk textile design has yet to be clearly defined. Mamluk silks and other textiles are exceedingly rare, and many of those that have survived have been retrieved from excavations of burials in Upper Egypt. Precious silks were used in the production of honorary robes, diplomatic gifts and high-class articles produced especially for export. Striped silks were particularly popular, and frequently the names and titles of sultans were incorporated into the design. Areas of Production for textiles such as this one included Asyut, a town in Upper Egypt, well-known for its high-quality linens and silks. Silks inscribed with the benediction ‘Honour to al-Ashraf’ are amongst the latest datable fabrics of the Mamluk era, the V&A in London holding several fragments with this feature.  
It has been suggested that fabrics such as this one may have been produced during the reign of Sultan Qaytbay (AH 872–901 / AD 1468-96), whose official titles included ‘al-Ashraf’. Interestingly, blue textiles were often worn by *dhimmis* (the religious minorities)in the Mamluk period. Thus, a Coptic bishop buried at Qasr Ibrim in Upper Egypt, for example, was found wrapped in a blue-black woolen cloak.
20111b76-70e4-5b40-874b-20a4d142f81d.short_description: Mamluk silks are rare, but we know that they were used in the production of honorary robes, diplomatic gifts and high-class articles produced for export. Many bear the names and titles of sultans and this piece is assumed to have been produced during the reign of Sultan Qaytbay (AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96).
20111b76-70e4-5b40-874b-20a4d142f81d.method_for_datation: Mamluk silk fragments bearing the inscription ‘Honour to al-Ashraf’ are assumed to have been produced during the reign of Sultan Qa’itbay (872–901 / 1468–96). Stylistically, motifs on this silk fragment can also be compared with those occurring on contemporary metalwork.
20111b76-70e4-5b40-874b-20a4d142f81d.method_for_provenance: This item was retrieved from a tomb at al-Drounka, Egypt and can be classified as having been produced in Mamluk Egypt on the basis of stylistic comparison with other Mamluk textile fragments.

20111b76-70e4-5b40-874b-20a4d142f81d.obtention: This piece together with several other Fatimid fragments were acquired by the NMS from Henry Wallis in 1898. Wallis was a famous Pre-Raphaelite painter, who travelled and painted extensively in Egypt and elsewhere. Subsequently he became a highly respected expert on Egyptian and Persian ceramics.

24d1b22a-7e02-5a13-97d1-ffbb62d62561.name: Fragment from the internal *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba
24d1b22a-7e02-5a13-97d1-ffbb62d62561.short_description:
This fragment comes from the internal *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba which was presented by the Ottoman sultan ‘Abdülaziz (r. 1861–1876) in his first regnal year. It was the last internal *kiswa* to be sent by the Ottomans. It remained inside the Ka‘ba until 1936, when it was replaced by an Indian-made one. Later internal kiswas were woven in Mecca.  
The section preserved in fragment represents almost half of the loom width and an almost complete vertical repeat. The latter is made up of four zigzag bands. In the first wide band is the *shahada*, followed in a narrower band by phrases in praise of God. The third band has cartouches and roundels inscribed with invocations to God. The final narrow band has *sura* *al-Baqara*, II, verse 144, in part, ‘*We see the turning of thy face (for guidance) to the heavens: now shall We turn thee to a Qibla that shall please thee. Turn then thy face in the direction of the sacred Mosque*’.

24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.name: Flag
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.short_description: A piece of green Syrian silk fabric, inset on the top of the mast, which used to be carried during religious ceremonies. Trade and crafts were common activities in Jordan between the late 19th century and the earlier 20th century. These activities depended on migration and attracted groups of people who travelled or settled in the Jordanian territory to produce or sell products. Thus, the exchange of goods among different areas was very common, as exemplified by this object and many traditional dresses. Silk textiles were very common products in the Jordanian and Palestinian areas and were purchased from Syria, being an element in local fashion, both in Jordan and in Palestine.

2a768548-ee78-5645-b436-21f2d9bcf5cd.name: Fragment of woven linen.
2a768548-ee78-5645-b436-21f2d9bcf5cd.description: A linen textile fragment comprising a horizontal panel of embroidered decoration with a repeat composition of two wider sections that alternate twice with two narrow sections. These are separated from each other by double borders in black wove. The wider panels have alternating blue and purple cursive inscriptions bordered by scrolling bands above and below. The narrow sections contain S-scrolls arranged vertically, beneath which is a continuous border of alternating inverted crescents and circles.
2a768548-ee78-5645-b436-21f2d9bcf5cd.short_description: Many Fatimid and Mamluk textiles have been found in burials in Upper Egypt, an area famous for its linen-weaving industry manned by Coptic Christian as well as Muslim textile workers. This textile was collected by Henry Wallis (1830–1916), a famous painter and expert on Middle Eastern ceramics.

2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.name: Fragment from a tiraz.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.description:
This beige-coloured linen fragment is decorated with two horizontal strips of calligraphy embroidered in green silk. The inscription is in *kufic* lettering with split uprights.  
The beginning and end of both inscriptions are missing. In spite of its damaged condition, one can read in the first line; 'May the blessing of God fall on Muhammad the highest of all prophets and on his good and pious ancestors.'  
On the second line is written; '(There is no other divinity) than God in his oneness and may blessings fall on Muhammad the highest of all prophets.'  
The *tiraz* was made using a weaving technique typical of the Egyptian textile industry up to the end of the Fatimid era. Its texture indicates that it was probably part of a *caliph*'s turban. It appears to have been made in a private workshop (*tiraz al-khassa*), reserved for the *caliph* and government dignitaries, rather than in a popular workshop (*tiraz al-amma*). The workshop would have been in the Nile Delta area, one that specialised in linen, and which was probably located in Alexandria, Damiette, Tinnis or Dabiq.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.short_description: Fragment of beige linen from a *tiraz* made using a needlework technique employed in the Egyptian textile industry during the Fatimid period. The texture of the *tiraz* suggests that it was made in a workshop reserved for use by the caliph and the important dignitaries of the regime.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.dates: Hegira, last quarter of the 4th–first third of the 5th centuries / AD 10th–11th centuries.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.method_for_datation: Comparison with other similar pieces of cloth with identical inscriptions referring to the family and good, pious ancestors of the Prophet shows that this piece belonged to an Egyptian Fatimid *caliph*. The absence of exuberant decoration combining geometric, floral and animal motifs would place the date between the last quarter of the 4th and the first third of the 5th century / 10th–11th century.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.method_for_provenance: The weaving method and the ownership by a Fatimid *caliph* both indicate that the cloth was made in Egypt.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.obtention: The *tiraz* was bought in 1958 by the late H. H. Abdelwahab, former Director of the National Institute of Art and Archaeology, from an Egyptian antique dealer. He then donated it to the Ribat Museum at Monastir.
2dd5e058-db6d-5ca4-b1c8-b47beedc0811.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Tiraz; calligraphy; Fatimid textiles; workshop; embroidery

33c038eb-514c-5d28-8576-edfccf3f87e8.name: Fragment of silk lampas with geometric pattern
33c038eb-514c-5d28-8576-edfccf3f87e8.short_description:
Since the 12th century, Granada has been the leading centre of the Pyrenees for the production of high quality silk. This costly golden-thread silk lampas dated to the 14th century could be used as interior decoration in one of the Granada palaces. A very similar fabric is known to be used for interior decoration in the famous Alhambra Palace.  
The geometric pattern includes favourite Muslim motifs: octagonal stars and rosettes, braids, stylized plant elements. Historians suppose the common origin of the textile décor with that of Nasrid architecture and, first of all, with the carved and mosaic ornamental panels of Alhambra.  
Quite rare is the motif of paired heraldic birds sitting in the tree branches. It may be hypothetically considered as an image of Simurg (Senmurv), the holy King of the birds in the folklore of Iranians and Turks. The literate Muslims of Nasrid Spain were well versed in the key narratives of the Near and Middle East culture due to Arabic translations of books, particularly of Abu l-Qasim Ferdowsi's poem Book of Kings ("*Shahnama*").

34a076dd-a17c-5255-8e20-be760dc55f04.name: Kilim (fragment)
34a076dd-a17c-5255-8e20-be760dc55f04.description: The fragment shown here is the upper right corner of a two-panel, large format Central Anatolian kilim, of which only this part of one panel has survived. Such pieces were produced for personal use and were part of the dowry. They served primarily as a representative cover for bedding and containers and were stacked directly opposite the tent entrance, clearly visible to any guest entering the tent. The fragment of this white-ground Konya kilim, with its massive hook motif, features individual scattered motifs in brocaded technique, which indicate the weaving direction of this slit tapestry. It shows the subdued coloration typical of the Konya region in the early 19th century.

In the last decade before the Berlin Wall came down Müller collected oriental rugs, carpets and flat weaves for the Ethnographic Museum of Dresden in the Dresden-Leipzig-Berlin region to secure remaining rural and nomadic textiles from the 19th and beginning 20th century. 35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.name: Textile with prayer niche (*mihrab*).
35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.description: The fabric, made of red, black and yellow-brown silk, is decorated with motifs embroidered with silver- and gold-plated copper wire woven into a cotton base. 3617cdf7-a6c7-5a09-b369-f188ba752294.name: Two fragments of brocade with parrot, butterfly, deer and hare pattern
3617cdf7-a6c7-5a09-b369-f188ba752294.short_description: Two nearly equal in size square-shaped fragments of figured silk brocade are stitched together on a support. "A flower and a bird", a favourite love theme in Persian culture, is further developed here through adding images of butterfly, deer and hare. Incorrectness in scales of animals indicates a semantic hierarchy in which the bird and the flower remain the most important.  Persian silver and golden-thread brocades and other elite textiles were the key item of Iranian artistic production and exports during the Safavid era, being the height of fashion both among Iranian and European aristocracy, as well as Christian clergy.

38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.name: Curtain for the *minbar* of the Meccan sanctuary, with the name of King Faruq I of Egypt
38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.short_description:
This is an exceptionally fine example of the high quality of embroidery produced by the craftsmen of Dar al-Kiswa in the mid 20th century. Very few curtains for the Meccan *minbar* survive, and none of the known examples predates the early 20th century. This is probably one of the last ones made, as Egypt stopped sending curtains for the Meccan *minbar* around that time.  
  
The top panel is inscribed, ‘God Almightly said in his revered book’. The three lines below have *sura al-Jumu‘a* (LXII), verse 9, which appropriately mentions the call to prayer on Fridays. The last panel states that ‘This sitara for the minbar of the sacred House of God was ordered by him who depends on God, the king of Egypt Faruq I, may God grant him succor, in the year 1365’.

4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.name: Mahmal
4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.short_description:
This ceremonial *mahmal* consists of a tent-like cotton cloth embroidered with gold and silver threads. Placed upon a wooden frame (litter) on a camel’s back, the *mahmal* would bear the *kiswa* (Kaaba covering) and other religious items to Mecca in a pilgrimage procession.  
  
This example from Ottoman Turkey features the Mamluk yellow colour embellished with the Throne verse *(Ayat al-Kursi)*, the Muslim invocation (*Basmala*), and the declaration of faith *(Shahada)* in *thuluth* calligraphy. The signature of the Ottoman sultan is visible in *tughra* script.  
  
During the *hajj* or pilgrimage season, the caravan would parade the streets of Cairo in a festival accompanied by musicians before embarking on the journey to Saudi Arabia. The *mahmal* reminds of a wedding procession and carries feminine connotations through its familiarity with the *howdaj* used to transport women hidden away from the public eye.  
  
Muslim rulers would commission a *mahmal* in an opportunity to highlight their sovereignty, taste and piety. Although the legend of Mamluk Sultanah Fatima Shajarat al-Durr associated the ruler with the first *mahmal*, scholars debate the first appearance with earlier references recounting Zubaydah, the wife of Harum al Rashid, using a palanquin in a pilgrimage procession from Baghdad to Mecca.

4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.name: Pearl Diver’s Nose Clip
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.short_description: This simple, but effective nose clip, known as futam (pl. aftama) in the Gulf region, was traditionally made of horn, wood or occasionally tortoise shell. Historical sources reaching back to the 4th century H/ 10th century AD already describe the clips' distinctive 'arrow' or 'scissor' shape, which remained largely unchanged until modern times. Equipped only with his noseclip, finger guards (khubat), occasionally a protective suit against jelly fish (libas al-ghaws) and a basket or bag (dyyin) for the oysters, a pearl diver would descend 50-60 times every day to bring up as many oysters as he could.

461e1b34-d976-5ed9-8d53-d69810250d6c.name: Tomb cover.
461e1b34-d976-5ed9-8d53-d69810250d6c.description:
A woven silk tomb cover that has a repeat design of zigzag bands set against a dark-green ground. Each zigzag band is contained within narrow borders that hold repetitions of the *shahada*, the Islamic profession of faith, rendered in white with red outlines and set against a dark-green ground: ‘La Ilah Ila Illah wa Muhammad rasul Illah’ (‘There is no God but God and Muhammad is the Messenger of God’). The narrow borders above contain prayers for the Prophet, while those below contain prayers for the four righteous caliphs Abu Bakr, ‘Umar, ‘Uthman and ‘Ali as well as for the companions of the Prophet. In between the bands the superposed words ‘Allah’ and ‘Muhammad’ are repeated.  
In Ottoman Turkey the cenotaphs of important personages were often draped with various types of textiles, much like this one, with its zigzag patterns of calligraphic prayers. It has been suggested that these textiles may have been intended to recall the ceremonial drapery or *kiswa* covering the Holy Ka’ba in Mecca. The earliest textiles of this type have been dated to the AH 11th / AD 17th century, and the latest to the AH 13th / AD 19th century.
461e1b34-d976-5ed9-8d53-d69810250d6c.short_description: In Ottoman Turkey the cenotaphs of important individuals were often draped with religious textiles showing a distinctive design of zigzag panels containing Qur’anic prayers. This custom may have been intended to recall the ceremonial draping of the Holy Ka’ba in Mecca with the so-called *kiswa* cover.
461e1b34-d976-5ed9-8d53-d69810250d6c.method_for_datation: A stylistically related funerary textile is in the V&A, London (inv. no. 780-1892), and there is another in the Topkapı Palace Museum (inv. no. 13/1690), both have been dated to the 11th / 17th century (see Atasoy *et. al*, 2000; *Türkische Kunst*, 1985).
461e1b34-d976-5ed9-8d53-d69810250d6c.method_for_provenance: Funerary textiles of this type are ascribed to Ottoman Turkey (see Atasoy *et. al*, 2000; *Türkische Kunst*, 1985).

461e827a-157a-5afd-aba7-850f0e156798.name: Banner
461e827a-157a-5afd-aba7-850f0e156798.short_description: Inscribed with the names of God, the Prophet Muhammad and the first four leaders of the Muslim community, and bordered by Qur’anic verses, this silk *sanjak* (shield-shaped banner) displays a two-bladed sword with a dragon-headed hilt. Referred to as Dhu’l Fiqar and associated with military victory, this sword is said to have belonged to ‘Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet. While Ottoman banners similar to this one were used as military insignia from the 15th century onward, this example bears an early 19th century date, and may have been borne instead by the faithful during pilgrimage to Mecca.

4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.name: Flag of the Italian Socialist Party’s local branch in a small village near Turin (Cafasse Torinese), bearing the image of a worker breaking a sword (an icon of antimilitarism)
4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.short_description:
The Italian Socialist Party opposed Italian participation in World War I. After the government and the King decided to enter the war on the side of French and Britain, the Socialist’s Party line became “né aderire, né sabotare” (neither support, nor sabotage). Anti-war sentiments remained widespread among workers and peasants. In August 1917, without any prior organisation by the Socialist Party or by the trade union, spontaneous bread riots erupted in Turin: women led marchers that demanded bread and the end of the war, and they looted shops and barracks. Such protests were harshly repressed.  
War casualties were very high: 650,000 military deaths, 950,000 wounded, 600.000 prisoners of war or missing.
4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.author: Giulia Barrera

48f83022-a45d-5b11-b4e5-88c259a5ca69.name: Textile fragment
48f83022-a45d-5b11-b4e5-88c259a5ca69.short_description: This textile exhibits bands of varying patterns including interlacing calligraphic inscriptions. Here, the texts convey wishes for happiness, good fortune and prosperity. The hues of the brightly-coloured fragment, with its contrasting red, green and gold, characterize the textiles produced during the Nasrid and later periods in Spain and North Africa. Its appearance is in sharp contrast to textiles produced in earlier periods, which exhibit a lighter, more delicate palette of minty greens, light blues and a heavy use of golden metal-wrapped threads.

4a45199e-3af5-504d-9932-a1e4ed67dc93.name: Printed cotton textile fragment.
4a45199e-3af5-504d-9932-a1e4ed67dc93.description:
This cotton textile fragment is decorated with a printed design distributed along two bands. The upper band is narrow and consists of a repeated inscription in Mamluk *thuluth* script which reads: 'Al-sabr ni'm al-nasir li kul shay'in akhir' ('Patience is blessed with success and everything has an end'). The inscription is executed in a style where the letters are interwoven and the bases are raised in such a manner that equidistant spaces are created between them. These spaces are adorned by decorative units consisting of plaited lines in the form of braids.  
The lower band is wider than the upper and decorated with ornamentation distributed along four rows, consisting of two repeating and alternating decorative units: an eight-pointed star and a circular form within which are two concentric circles. The stars and circles in each row are organised so that the arrangement in the preceding row is opposite to that which follows. Each star is decorated with stylised floral designs, whereas the outer circle of the roundel is ornamented with a braided pattern, followed on the inside by a series of consecutive dots, which are followed in turn by the decorative form called '*Dawama'* (vortex). This is a decorative form that was widespread in Mamluk art especially in ornamental metal objects.  
Egypt was famed for printed cotton textiles during the Mamluk period which was greatly influenced by trade with India, from where Egypt imported printed cotton clothing as well as raw cotton. The Mamluk craftsmen knew many different printing techniques, amongst which was wood-block printing with raised and sunken designs, and wax-resist wood-block printing. This textile fragment might have been part of a dress, curtain or perhaps more likely to have come from the cover of a counterpane, as it is comparable to a similar one housed in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo.
4a45199e-3af5-504d-9932-a1e4ed67dc93.short_description: The weaving industry in Mamluk Cairo included cotton and silk textiles. Some textiles were embroidered with silk while others, like this cotton piece, were block-printed. It bears a well-known expression indicating that patience is the best policy.
4a45199e-3af5-504d-9932-a1e4ed67dc93.method_for_datation: This textile fragment was dated based on the style of the inscription, written in the Mamluk *thuluth* script. The similarities of the decorative components on this piece to other designs, especially on dated metal objects, also helped to narrow the time frame of its manufacture, especially the decorative motif known as '*Dawama'*. Furthermore, the word 'Nasir' which appears in the inscription, might be an reference to Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who ruled in the latter half of the 7th / 13th century and throughout the first four decades – with the exception of almost one year – of the 8th / 14th century.
4a45199e-3af5-504d-9932-a1e4ed67dc93.method_for_provenance: The type of decorative motif found on this textile fragment was used frequently by Mamluk craftsmen. Furthermore Egypt was famed for its printed cotton textiles.
4a45199e-3af5-504d-9932-a1e4ed67dc93.obtention: The textile was purchased in 1928 from a dealer in antiquities, Albert Abimayo.

4ce02a11-07e9-50f5-a7d7-3651d7dd3510.name: Textile fragment with cockerel medallions.
4ce02a11-07e9-50f5-a7d7-3651d7dd3510.description: A plain-woven silk textile fragment thought to come from a shirt. The weave has a pattern inlaid with extra wefts of silver and gold strips in the manner of brocading. The colour scheme is predominantly red, with detailing in blue and yellow. The design consists of lozenge-shaped cartouches formed from individual flowers, these enclose octagons with red, yellow and blue outlines and a central cockerel, facing left. The spaces in between the lozenges are filled with decorative bands formed from an alternating pattern of large stars and small octagons with central star motifs.
4ce02a11-07e9-50f5-a7d7-3651d7dd3510.short_description: The Muslim world was famous for its textile production, which built on Sassanid and Byzantine traditions and soon excelled these in sophistication and complexity. Court-sponsored workshops in Iraq, Iran, Egypt and later Spain competed to produce the most splendid silks as symbols of power and wealth.
4ce02a11-07e9-50f5-a7d7-3651d7dd3510.method_for_datation: This textile has been dated tentatively to the 4th–5th / AD 11th–12th century on the basis of its clear stylistic relationship with post-Sasanian and early Islamic textiles.
4ce02a11-07e9-50f5-a7d7-3651d7dd3510.method_for_provenance: This textile has been associated with Abbasid Iraq on the basis of its clear stylistic relationship with post-Sassanid and early Islamic textiles from the region.

4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.name: Canopy with lotus roundels
4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.short_description:
A spectacular example of Indian silk weaving, this textile has possibly the widest loom-width of any known samite. A textile such as this, with a width in excess of 3 metres, would have stretched the effort and expense of drawloom weaving to their limits. Apart from the extreme technical difficulty of weaving a samite of this scale, the very high quality of yarns, dyes and workmanship suggest that it could have been woven only in the controlled production environment of a royal workshop.  
A textile of this size would have been used as a canopy or ceiling cloth for a congregation hall or chapel at one of Tibet’s Buddhist establishments. However, this particular example, with its abstract roundels, could have served equally well as the ceiling of a royal tent at any Indian court.

517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.name: Textile Panel
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.short_description: Most of the textiles that survive from Fatimid Egypt, mainly fragments, were made or reused as burial shrouds and were preserved on account of the dryness of the Egyptian climate. This comparatively large panel may therefore derive from a funerary context; to compensate for areas of loss, it appears to have been pieced together in modern times from four parts of the same cloth, suggesting the original panel was once much longer. Its materials (bleached linen and silk), tapestry-weave technique, and bands of geometric decoration all mark it as a product of the Fatimid period. There are several bands of inscription that can be read as a repetition of “Help from Allah,” but because it lacks a royal or historical inscription, this cloth was likely made for a humbler clientele rather than for the ruling elite. However, it is otherwise very similar in style and manufacture to the so-called Cadouin Shroud (Abbey of Cadouin, France), inscribed in the name of the caliph al-Musta‘lī (r. Hegira 487-495/ AD 1094–1101).

517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.name: Tiraz
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.short_description: Textiles from the first centuries of the Islamic era survive mainly in the form of fragments, including *tiraz*, with their characteristic embroidered or woven inscriptions supplying the name and titles of the ruler. Such cloth was produced in state factories and was the exclusive preserve of the caliph. This piece belongs to the Tulunid period (Hegira 254–292 / AD 868–905) in Egypt, where most of the surviving *tiraz* were discovered. It is one of the largest such examples; however, the inscription is too fragmentary to be read.

517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.method_for_datation: The linen is undyed while the wool wefts are mustard, olive green and black, which are all typical of the Tulunid period. The letters comprising the *kufic* text are consonant with Tulunid architectural inscriptions as for example the wood inscribed panels from the mosque of Ibn Tulun, in Fustat, completed in Hegira 265 / AD 879.
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.method_for_provenance: Most surviving *tiraz* come from Egypt, in this instance perhaps from a workshop of the Nile Delta.

54253d73-c552-552c-b44e-749462babb24.name: Embroidered linen.
54253d73-c552-552c-b44e-749462babb24.description:
An embroidered textile thought to have served either as a cover for a divan (low sofa seat); a quilt facing; or as a hanging such as a curtain for a door. It is made up of three vertical lengths of linen sewn together and embroidered. The composition of wavy stems, leaves and tulips is inspired by AH 10th- and 11th- / AD 16th- and 17th-century Ottoman velvets, brocades and woven silks. The silk-thread colours of red, green, blue and yellow are typical of the time; the stitch used is a regular darning stitch with the length of four counted threads over the linen, and one under it. Red dominates the composition, covering most of the stems, all of the tulips, and some of the leaves. The blue is used on the leaves and the green is used to embroider the bases of the tulips and some of the stems. The yellow, which has largely faded, is used to fill in some of the gaps between all the other colours in the shapes of strokes and small buds. This textile has a border designed with a row of smaller red tulips and green stems with blue leaves, and yellow strokes and buds which alternate in their leaning, bending once to the right and once to the left.  
  
Silk embroidery of the AH 11th / AD 17th century was a cheaper option for those who wanted to enjoy sumptuous textiles, given that woven-silk fabrics were much more expensive. It is sometimes difficult to distinguish between embroideries made by women at home and those worked by men in workshops for the trade. The pattern on this embroidery indicates that it was most probably made professionally in a workshop, because the pattern relates strongly to similar designs found on AH 10th- and 11th- / AD 16th- and 17th-century velvets.
54253d73-c552-552c-b44e-749462babb24.short_description: This boldly embroidered linen textile with coloured silk threads may have been used as a cover for a divan, a quilt facing, or a hanging such as a curtain for a doorway. Lavishly embroidered pieces that are influenced by velvets, like this one, were relatively more affordable than woven-silk fabrics.
54253d73-c552-552c-b44e-749462babb24.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the pattern of this embroidery relates strongly to those appearing on 10th- and 11th- / 16th- and 17th-century Ottoman velvets.
54253d73-c552-552c-b44e-749462babb24.method_for_provenance: The pattern of this embroidery relates strongly to those appearing on Turkish Ottoman velvets.

550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.name: Bridal cushions (background: Maan section of Hijaz Railroad, Jordan)
550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.description: Bridal cushions from Ma’an, Jordan, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, are among the most distinctive examples of Jordanian domestic textiles. Their fabrics and techniques reflect connections with textile traditions from the Caucasus, Syria, Turkey, and Central Asia, shaped through centuries of travel, trade, pilgrimage, and cultural exchange. These influences reached Ma’an through its position as an important crossroads on regional routes, particularly as a key stop along the Hejaz Railway, built during the Ottoman period to facilitate travel between Damascus and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The background image is from the G. Eric and Edith Matson Photograph Collection at the Library of Congress, showing the Hejaz Railway, which connected communities across the Ottoman Empire and facilitated movement for travellers, pilgrims, and merchants between the Levant and the Hijaz.

55bb16e8-b3ef-5f94-b1f1-f81a6e6d3cb7.name: Textile fragment with *cintamani* motifs
55bb16e8-b3ef-5f94-b1f1-f81a6e6d3cb7.short_description: The silk fragment with red ground is patterned with horizontally aligned, offset waved lines. Growing out of these is a stylised bunch of flowers, its centre formed by a pink. The waved lines together form three circles arranged into a triangle, the Ottoman *cintamani* motif, which on this silk fragment is additionally flanked by two cloud bands.

568aa288-3d05-5bf2-9461-11f5d3c78666.name: *Portrait of Charles of Bourbon*
568aa288-3d05-5bf2-9461-11f5d3c78666.description:
The Portrait of Charles of Bourbon (Charles III of Spain), one of a pair together with a portrait depicting Queen Maria Amalia of Saxony, now lost, is one of the first creations of the Royal Tapestry Factory in Naples.  
Founded by the young King in 1737, soon after his arrival in Naples, the tapestry factory, together with a factory for the carving of semiprecious stones, was one of the first established by order of Charles of Bourbon. This decision must have been influenced by the young Charles’ interest in the Medici factories that were still operating in Florence. This interest developed when the future King stayed in the city in 1732, as the future successor to Gian Gastone de’ Medici.  
In fact, a small group of Florentine weavers and carvers of precious stones was responsible for giving life to the first two royal Bourbon factories in Naples, located near the church of San Carlo alle Mortelle. The factory, which was also composed of a local workforce, with the aim of promoting the development of new artistic techniques in the Kingdom of Naples, was under the direction of the Florentine Domenico del Rosso. And it was to the Florentine weaver that Charles entrusted his portrait and that of his consort; as with other items produced during the initial phase of the factories, these works were intended to celebrate the King and their patron. Production of the tapestry was completed in 1741, as indicated by the presence of the signature and date on the bottom right-hand edge of the tapestry: “DOM.CO D. L. ROSSO 1741”. The artist who provided the preparatory study for the tapestry is unknown; however, there is speculation that it may have been Giovan Battista delle Piane, who was a court portrait painter during these years; or Francesco Solimena, based on the tapestry’s extraordinary expressiveness and the intensity of the light and the colours in its original state.

58b6fce0-a922-5b62-a0f4-e670ee6e41c9.name: Banner
58b6fce0-a922-5b62-a0f4-e670ee6e41c9.short_description:
The earliest of the complete Ottoman banners in the Khalili Collection, the central motif on this banner is the sword Dhu’l-Faqar, represented with the dragon quillons usually seen in its depiction on Ottoman banners. The inscription on the bifurcated blade is *sura* *al-Nisa’* (IV), verses 95 (end) and 96. This is surrounded by calligraphic medallions enclosing the names of God, Muhammad and the four Orthodox Caliphs, each with the appropriate invocation, and *sura* *Hud* (XI), part of verse 88.  
  
The banner can be dated to the 17th century on the basis of its close resemblance in iconography and technique to a number of securely dated military trophies in European collections. Many copies of early banners, made in Istanbul in the early 19th century, can easily be identified by the incorporation in their design of a small calligraphic flag, thought to represent the Prophet’s own standard.

58fd0ec7-5172-5bbf-bac4-88e40da41359.name: Alpujarra Rug or Bedcover
58fd0ec7-5172-5bbf-bac4-88e40da41359.description:
The Alpujarra rugs (or bedcovers) with pile in loops were produced in the Alpujarra region south of Granada between the 15th-16th and the 19th centuries. Alpujarra rugs or covers are classified as European folk art and were influenced by Eastern rugs.  
The cover was woven in three parts on a narrow beam loom, then stitched together. The weaver used only three colours of mercerized cotton (ivory, abrashed saffron yellow and light green) and metal thread. The yellow ground field is adorned with a diagonal lattice with green and ivory rosettes in the rhombuses. A two-headed eagle with a crown is in the centre. On the lower edge of the field in the inscription “DOÑA ROSALIA BTAVO” (BRAVO?). The border is green and has a crowned lion in each of the four corners. Between the lions is an alternating pattern of rosettes and pairs of doves atop bowls. The outer border contains stylised lilies alternating with star rosettes.  
Alfréd Hoffman, owner of *Eggenberger*, one of the oldest book companies in Pest (founded in 1768), donated the bedcover in 1894 to the Museum of Applied Arts in accordance with the will of friend, János Kovachich-Molnár (1838-1894), who had been his business partner since 1863.

5c6bfb8e-5045-5559-8078-f4e37350944b.name: Pillowcase
5c6bfb8e-5045-5559-8078-f4e37350944b.short_description: Textiles and embroidery found a wide array of uses which reflect the imaginations of Turkish women. In these textiles, silk, golden and silver threads were used for embroidery. From the 18th and 19th century on – when Western influence started – almost every colour found use and by using different tones of the same colour, the illusion of light and depth was created. Instead of human and animal figures, floral design, fruits, or calligraphy, ship and architectural patterns became more popular. This piece was made in the Hereke Plant, founded in 1843. There is one big star and crescent in the middle while there are four smaller ones in the corners. The base is covered with plenty of stars and dots.

5d84c4b0-6f1a-5b1c-87d0-3d8a61317a0a.short_description:
During the second half of the 19th century, “friendly societies” flourished in Italy (especially in Central and Northern Italy). They predated trade unionism and were an important element of Italian social life.  
The Female Friendly Society (Società di mutuo soccorso femminile) of Cremona was created in 1863. It mostly comprised factory workers such as spinners and other workers in textile industry, but also included craftswomen like self-employed dressmakers, and even a few teachers.

5e3bd511-e913-550c-a38c-80f8d87cf0e9.name: *Capture of Francis I, King of France*
5e3bd511-e913-550c-a38c-80f8d87cf0e9.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
The central episode represented in the tapestry is the capture of Francis I. After having passed through the copse, depicted high up on the left, and after having fought bravely on the muddy terrain, unfavourable to the heavy French cavalry, the King is captured following a shot from an arquebus that wounds his horse.  
Francis I is depicted in the foreground while three cavaliers from the enemy formation, La Motte de Noyers, the German Nicolas von Salm and the Count of Montmartin – as indicated by the abbreviated text that tends to be included on the horses’ tack and armour – help him to get to his feet. On the left is depicted the Viceroy of Naples, Charles de Lannoy, identified by the letters “VISSEROV” on the blade of his sword, while he dismounts from his horse to accept the surrender of the King.  
Behind him a horseman raises the imperial standard, on which one can distinguish the double-headed eagle and Hercules’ pillars with the motto “PLUS OVLTRE”. In the centre of the tapestry, the man on a horse, who is wearing a dark outfit, on which stands out the white cross that indicates that he is on the side of the French, is Henry II, King of Navarre, captured in battle; in the distance, on the right, among the horsemen who have just come out of the copse, appears Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, identified by the word “BOURBON” on the reins, as well as by the presence of French *fleurs-de-lis* on the horse’s peytral.  
In the foreground, on the ground, there is the arquebus with which Francis I’s horse was hit. This is also a symbol of the new way of fighting in battle and the end of the cavalry: the use of firearms, striking from a distance, allowed the less courageous to prevail.

5e6943fd-7101-58f0-8df8-80cc6f82f37e.name: *Advance of the imperial troops and attack of the French gendarmerie led by Francis I*
5e6943fd-7101-58f0-8df8-80cc6f82f37e.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries of the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections with the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Through the decorative cycle of tapestries, the intention was to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, commanded by Francis I, which took place on 24 February 1525, and was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia. Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels and to adorn a large room in the Royal Palace to mark the occasion of the Assembly of the Estates-General of Brussels in March 1531, the cycle arrived in Spain in the 1550s with Mary of Hungary, who later gave it to her young nephew Don Carlos. It is Don Carlos who links the history of the tapestries to the d’Avalos family, bequeathing them to Francesco Ferdinando d’Avalos (Buchanan 2002), Marquis of Pescara, and direct descendant of Fernando Francesco d’Avalos, the hero of Pavia depicted in the tapestry *Defeat of the French cavalry* and identified thanks to the writing on the neck of his horse.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris), a renowned painter, and designer of tapestries and stained-glass windows. The preparatory cartoons for the weaver were derived from these designs, or *modelletti*, with scenes reversed, given that, at the time in Brussels, tapestries were woven on “low-warp” looms. The presence of the weaver’s mark on the border of two of the tapestries provides a reference point for when the series was produced, because a decree of 1528 required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and this has allowed the workshop in which they were made to be identified as that of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen).  
The initial stages of the battle are represented in the tapestry. In the background, the infantry and cavalry of the imperial army are advancing, led by Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, Constable of France (recognisable from the writing on his horse’s peytral), ready to attack the French troops. On the right, in the middle distance, King Francis I is depicted in the act of killing the Marquis of Civita Santangelo, commander of the enemy troops, an event that marks one of the first French successes. In the extreme foreground, on the right, several imperial arquebusiers can be seen preparing their weapons: across their shoulders, they wear a strap from which hang pouches containing gunpowder charges that have already been measured out; at their waists they have horn-shaped powder magazines. The legs of the arquebusier seen from behind, which are cut off at the knee, were originally hidden by a section of the wall of Visconti Park, as is also shown by the preparatory drawing for the tapestry, now in the Louvre. This section of wall could have been removed together with the border of the tapestry, no earlier than the second half of the 18th century. In fact, according to a description from the 1770s, the lower border, still intact, displayed decorative motifs with tritons and sea horses, similar to those that appear in the *Hunts of Maximilian*, another series of tapestries produced for Charles V from designs by van Orley, and today in the Louvre (Buchanan 2002).  
In the foreground, the King is depicted again, with his sallet visor lowered, as he heads with his elite guard towards a copse, where a fatal trap will be set for him.

5e9b4b02-68df-5a5e-b287-ce07332661a1.short_description: Typical products of the Qajar dynastic period, the Persian term *qalamkar* (literally, “pen-work“) refers to printed or/and painted cotton fabrics decorated with animals, depictions of Persian heroic fables, floral and tendril patterns or cypresses growing out of vases. Depending on the motif, *qalamkars* were employed as fabric for clothing, wall hangings or table cloths. The most famous member of this dynasty, Naser ad-Din Shah, visited the Vienna World’s Fair in 1873.

618bc97a-0543-5e59-aeff-839fc23ec12e.name: *Sitara* for the *rawda* of the Prophet’s mosque in Medina
618bc97a-0543-5e59-aeff-839fc23ec12e.short_description:
That this curtain was intended for the *rawda* is suggested by the text in the large medallion at the top. It consists of a *hadith* of the Prophet, *ma bayna qabri wa minbari rawda min riyad al-janna* (‘Between my tomb and my minbar is one of the gardens of Paradise’). The same text appears above the *mihrab* in the *rawda*.  
Sultan Mahmud II is known to have practised the art of calligraphy and a number of *sitara*s commissioned by him for the Prophet’s mosque bear his pear-shaped signature cartouche which reads, *katabahu al-‘abd Mahmud bin ‘Abdulhamid khan* (‘written by the servant \[of God\] Mahmud, the son of ‘Abdulhamid Khan’).

6392fda5-b738-5dec-9a45-71733b02404b.name: Tent panel
6392fda5-b738-5dec-9a45-71733b02404b.short_description: This appliqué is one of a set of six featuring designs that echo the bold geometry of Egypt’s period of Mamluk rule (1250–1517). This particular textile features the following verse from the Qur’an: “That man can have nothing but what he strives for...” (53:39). Appliqués of this type were often used to embellish tents.

64ac8dbf-8dd2-5b1c-a223-2129d475ce2e.name: Case for the crown of Stefan Bocskai
64ac8dbf-8dd2-5b1c-a223-2129d475ce2e.short_description: This decagonal domed case is made of wood and covered with fabric. The clasp at the front and the hinges at the back are silver-gilt. The fabric of the cover is costly Persian silk and is decorated with a figural scene surrounded by flowers. Half sitting, half reclining, a lady is reading a book. Beside her kneels a servant with a wide, sweeping *turban*, offering her a bowl with his right hand and holding a bottle in his left. Between the two figures lies a bowl containing fruit. In the lady's open book can be read the signature of the artist Mu'min, in Arabic script. On the inside of the case, the fabric retains all the freshness of its original colours, and is typical of the refined taste of the court of Shah 'Abbas the Great (AD 1587–1628) at Isfahan. Technically, it can be described as a double-woven lampas of coloured silk. Glued to the floor of the case is an Italian fabric from the early 17th century. Its ground is warp satin in red silk; the pattern, which takes the form of pinnate leaves and blossoms, is yellow silk woven in twill and intervowen with silver.

665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.name: Piece of the *kiswa* (cover) of the Ka’ba.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.description:
A piece of the Ka'ba *kiswa* (cover) which was probably produced in Syria, and was sent as part of the *Shami mahmal* (the Syrian Caravan carrying gifts for the Ka'ba) to Mecca to re-adorn the Ka'ba. Such a ritual occurred every year before the season of the Hajj, and included a venerated ceremony at which the commencement of the Hajj season was officially announced. It was and still is the case that the Ka'ba is washed, perfumed and purified every year and is then covered with a new *kiswa*. The fragmentexhibited here is made from red silk and embroidered with silver silken thread. The design includes two undulating bands which assume the form of a continuous chain made up of number “7”s. Both bands run from the beginning to the end of the cloth. Small, dispersed decorative elements are scattered between the two borders, as well as between the two undulating bands. Written inscriptions appear, the most prominent being: “There is no God but God and Muhammad is his Prophet”, repeating in the middle of the *kiswa* between the two zigzag bands. The two expressions, “Ya Mannan” (“Oh Merciful”) and “Ya Hannan” (“Oh Compassionate”) are also repeated, and consist of flowery forms running along both edges. On the upper undulating band, there is a verse from the Qur'an, “al-Baqara” (“the Cow”, 2: 144). The lower undulating band holds another chapter from the Qur'an: Surat Al 'Imran “the Family of Imran” (3:96). At the top and the bottom of the piece there are two expressions: “Dhu al-Jalal” (“Possessor of Majesty”) and “Dhu al-Ikram” (“Possessor of Honour”). One can conceptualise the size of the complete *kiswa* by bringing to mind the enormous scale of the Ka'ba. It is likely that the forms and inscriptions on this piece were repeated on the *kiswa* in its entirety. The name of the donor, the date of production and the emporium where it was produced is not recorded; the evidence has probably been cut off.  
It is worth mentioning that once used to cover the Ka'ba, the *kiswa* was cut into small pieces and sent as gifts to different capitals and cities in the Islamic world to bestow blessing on them. Ruling palaces and councils contained pieces of the *kiswa*, which were used to confer legality and sanctity.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.short_description: Every year the Ka’ba is washed and covered with a *kiswa* (cover) marking the beginning of the Hajj season. This piece is of red silk and embroidered with silver silk forming fragmented zigzags that repeat from the beginning of the piece to its end. Small forms are scattered in different places within inscription bands.

6748859a-edf1-57f0-b773-2f77f78d2cad.name: Brocaded velvet
6748859a-edf1-57f0-b773-2f77f78d2cad.short_description: This luxurious cloth is woven in red silk velvet with silver metallic threads. Although strikingly modern-looking in design, this motif is ancient. Known as *chintamani*, it derives from the Sanskrit word ‘precious jewel'. The triple spot motif has long represented the Buddhist eternal wish-granting jewel, but the 'spots and stripes' motif is also found in Persian paintings of ancient kings wearing the skins of tigers and leopards, associating this motif with power, kingship and royalty.

69333e0f-47a7-51b4-ada7-d43aa30c07fe.name: Flag of the peasants’ league of a small village in Tuscany, central Italy
69333e0f-47a7-51b4-ada7-d43aa30c07fe.short_description:
Peasants’ leagues (Lega Contadina) were the first form of agricultural workers’ organisations. They flourished in Italy at the end of the nineteenth and beginning of the twentieth century.  
Ravi and Caldana are villages in the municipality of Gavorrano (a mine district in the province of Grosseto, Tuscany).  
In 1911, when the national trade union Confederazione Generale del Lavoro (CGdL) proclaimed a strike against Italy’s colonial war in Libya, the miners of the Gavorrano district participated in the strike.

6936e4f0-8dda-5065-9aac-81da03ff336e.short_description:
The large, stylized tulips make this textile a fine example of the highly original and magnificent patterns that were designed in the Ottoman court studios.

6bb34fe7-eaef-56c1-b556-3d1d89dfb069.name: Marriage tent
6bb34fe7-eaef-56c1-b556-3d1d89dfb069.short_description: A complete early 20th century Egyptian tent adorned with colourful textile panels in interior part. *Khayamiyya* or Egyptian art of tent-making is created using a hand-applique technique in which fabric pieces are cut, folded and skillfully hand-sewn to canvas, producing impressive tents and wall hangings. These vibrant textiles are widely used in ceremonial contexts such as weddings, funerals, street parties and religious events. This tent was used for the wedding of a daughter of the last Khedive of Egypt in 1903. It can be erected with the decoration reversed should it be thought more appropriate.

6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.short_description: The interior walls of the Shrine of the Prophet in the Madina were traditionally honoured with elaborate hangings. During the Ottoman period, it was customary for the Sultan to send hangings for the shrine  on the occasion of his ascension to the throne or when wear and tear demanded them to be replaced. The old  hangings were returned to Istanbul.Judging by their inscriptions, it has been suggested that  black-grounded Ottoman textiles like this one may have been commissioned specifically to cover the tomb of the Prophet (pbuh). In addition to qur'anic inscriptions, the calligraphic panels include a large green medallion with a hadith of the Prophet: ‘ (For) whosoever may visit my grave, my intercession will become an obligation’. Below, elaborate arabesque scrolling surrounds the emblem or tughra of the sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD), who commissioned this hanging.

6cfb6464-d160-543b-9056-10619a938fd8.name: Textile (possibly a cushion cover)
6cfb6464-d160-543b-9056-10619a938fd8.short_description: Dating to the mid-10th/mid-16th century, this richly embellished textile gives a vivid sense of the multihued opulence of the court of the Ottoman Sultan Süleyman (Hegira 926–972 / AD 1520–65). Possibly a cushion cover for a throne or a sofa, the crimson satin fabric is embroidered with silk, gold and silver thread. The bold blossoms and spiky leaves that typify the Ottoman court style are arranged, along with a quartet of lively roosters, around a complex eight-lobed medallion. The quality of the design, the fine embroidery and the lavish use of silver and gold metallic thread demonstrate the unrivalled level of excellence of Ottoman imperial textiles.
