6fa63cbf-0340-5e3e-8071-e07e6642fc87.name: Bib for the camel of the Egyptian *mahmal*
6fa63cbf-0340-5e3e-8071-e07e6642fc87.short_description:
The camel destined to carry the Egyptian *mahmal* was specially chosen for its appearance as much as for its strength. It was looked after by a special employee in Dar al-Kiswa, and was caparisoned in richly embroidered textiles while being paraded through the streets of Cairo and major cities on its way to Mecca and back.  
  
The Qur’anic inscription, *sura al-Nahl*, verse 7, is apposite. It reads, ‘And they carry your heavy loads to lands that you could not otherwise reach except with souls distressed. Truly, your Lord is full of Kindness, Most Merciful.’  
  
The cotton lining bears a stamped trade mark of a firm in Manchester, England, consisting of an open hand bearing a name, possibly Abraham Harawi, in Arabic.

The centre of the rectangular cushion cover shows a medallion flanked by *saz* leaves and pinks placed in a rectangle, around which tulips are also depicted besides the *saz* leaves and pinks. 757957ce-46d4-5799-8792-5f05be3e1e3f.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
757957ce-46d4-5799-8792-5f05be3e1e3f.short_description: This green and black silk textile is richly embroidered with silver and gilt metal threads. The centre displays six cartouches with thuluth inscriptions, followed below by a black niche with a central lamp motif. A border with trefoil scrolling surrounds the central panel. The inscriptions used on this textile clearly indicate that this textile was intended for the Prophet’s Mosque in Madina. The four main cartouches contain verse 56 from chapter 33 (Al-Ahzab) of the Holy Qur’an: ‘Allah sends His Salat (merciful blessings) on the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), and also His angels. O you who believe! Send your Salat on him and greet him with the Islamic way of greeting’. The inscriptions in the two cartouches below state that this curtain was ordered by the Ottoman sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD) and renewed by Efendi Abbas Hilmi, the last Khedive Pasha of Ottoman Egypt (1291 H/ 1874 AD – 1350 H/ 1931 AD) in 1321 H/ 1903 AD.

7b315354-8d00-5a9b-9462-8f8f378759d3.name: Rustam Slaying the White Div
7b315354-8d00-5a9b-9462-8f8f378759d3.short_description:
The overall layout of this hanging is reminiscent of courtly manuscript illustrations with its figure-rich inner field and the border on which birds and game cavort in lush vegetation. The somewhat naïve style of the figures suggests that this embroidery in chain stitch technique must have been made at the beginning of the 20th century.  
  
The central field depicts scenes from the life of Rustam, the most popular hero from Ferdausi’s national epic *Shahnama*, the Book of Kings. The scene in the lower third is the easiest to recognise. It shows Rustam slaying the White Div, the ruler of Mazandaran. Above this we probably see Rustam’s fight with Suhrab, one of the most tragic moments in the *Shahnama*. During the duel, Rustam slays the young man, who shows him a talisman as he dies and it is at that moment that Rustam realises that he has just killed his very own son. Meanwhile, the top scene shows an unspecified battle scene.  
  
Wall hangings fulfilled many functions in Persian houses, be it as decoration for niches or as curtains. In this case, it is even conceivable that the hanging was used in one of the many coffee and tea houses, serving as a backdrop for professional storytellers to illustrate their stories.

7c7a8c7a-41b6-5201-9026-cc3578b10664.name: Curtain Panel with Design of Horizontal Bands of Geometric Patterns and Arabic Inscriptions in *Kufic* Script
7c7a8c7a-41b6-5201-9026-cc3578b10664.short_description: A long rectangular brocaded silk panel displaying twenty-one bands of varying widths with patterns in yellow, blue or green, black, and white on a red ground. Two bands are exceptionally wide. One of these wide bands is filled with a yellow geometric arabesque that encloses six elaborate eight-pointed stars. The other displays a smaller, more tightly spaced version of the star motif. Two nearly-identical sections of nine narrow bands alternate with these wide bands. In the center of each nine-band section is a band with five yellow stars surrounded by interlacing lines of blue or green forming an Arabic inscription in *kufic* script, which reads in translation as "success and happiness." On either side of this wide band is a series of three narrow bands with alternating red and yellow arabesques on either side of a central band. It has a running white arabesque around cartouches (ovoid frames) with another Arabic inscription in *kufic* script, which reads in translation as "good luck and prosperity," that alternate with rosettes in red or red and green. This series of seven smaller bands is framed by thin bands of alternating serrated triangles; the triangles point up and down in different colors, either red on green or white on green. The bottom of the panel has a contrasting checkerboard motif in yellow, white, black and red, and ends in a band of red tassels.

7de42026-ed99-5288-a199-da1cae44d5fc.name: Caparison for a horse given by the Sultan of Morocco to the King of Italy, on the occasion of a visit to Italy of a Moroccan Ambassador in 1890
7de42026-ed99-5288-a199-da1cae44d5fc.short_description:
In 1890, the Sultan of Morocco sent Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi as an Ambassador to Italy. The Ambassador landed in Naples on June 7th and arrived by train in Rome on June 13th. At the railway station, he was received by the Mayor of Rome, the Prefect, and other authorities. A military band was playing and military men in high uniform were paraded in the station to greet the Ambassador.  
Outside the station, three of the King’s gala carriages were waiting for the Ambassador and a military unit was paraded in his honour. Some carabinieri in high uniform escorted the Ambassador to the hotel.  
Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi presented the King with gifts, including some superb horses that the King immensely appreciated. The King presented the Ambassador with a magnificent small gold and diamonds small box and a hunting rifle and gave gold watches to the members of his escort.

80da057a-50e4-5b41-a93e-f12cf060df80.name: *Invasion of the French camp and the taking of the Castle of Mirabello. Flight of the ladies and civilians following Francis I*
80da057a-50e4-5b41-a93e-f12cf060df80.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here precedes *Flight of the imperial troops from Pavia*, where the Lombard city is portrayed. In fact, juxtaposing the two tapestries, the landscape bordered in the foreground by the walls of Visconti Park can be re-created; furthermore, both in the foreground and in the distance, the defensive system that marks the edge of the French encampment, composed of a series of gabions, field fortifications comprising large baskets of entwined branches filled with earth, can be linked together.  
According to the chronology of events, the tapestry represents one of the early moments of the final phase of the battle: at dawn on 24 February, the imperial troops burst into the French encampment. The French had pitched camp within the Old Park, occupying the Mirabello Castle, a fortified hunting lodge, depicted in the background on the left. In the centre, several infantrymen are trying to save themselves by crossing the Vernavola river, using their pikes. Beyond the flames, which are caused by the explosion of casks of gunpowder, one can glimpse Francis I’s tent, decorated with the French *fleurs-de-lis*. In the foreground, through a breach in the wall, one can see the flight of soldiers and civilians who were with the French army that was camped there, among them ornately dressed women. In the distance, on the right, one can see tranquil scenes of camp life, with people busy preparing food and overseeing meals.

821764f8-832c-5dab-a096-4cb7b82143b8.name: Textile fragment from the shrine of San Librada, Sigüenza Cathedral
821764f8-832c-5dab-a096-4cb7b82143b8.short_description: This textile fragment displays a pattern of roundels bearing addorsed griffins with gazelles below their forelegs, within a border of pairs of fantastic animals. The interstitial motif consists of an eight-pointed star enclosing a rosette and surrounded by pairs of confronted quadrupeds. The pattern, popular in both Muslim and Byzantine worlds, recalls earlier silks of the eastern Mediterranean and, ultimately, of Central Asia. Silks of this type have been found in reliquaries of churches in Spain; they may be the "patterns with circles" of Almeria referred to in historical documents. These Islamic textiles were most likely brought to Sigüenza by Alfonso VII, in 1147 on the occasion of the victory over the Almoravids and the capture of Almeria.

82a76cf7-12e6-5f7e-accc-28e18a32a4e9.description: A wall hanging for a domestic interior comprising three widths of coarse, brownish linen sewn together and embroidered in blue, red, yellow and green coloured silks using darning stitch. The overall composition is of staggered abstracted carnations that alternate with paired tulips; these rise from a split stem with serrated leaves issuing from either side. A turquoise-blue scalloped border surrounds the central composition.

82ea9712-5e3e-5143-b91a-4afc4229d69e.short_description: Ottoman embroidery was used to decorate a wide range of clothing and household items such as towels, waistbands, turban covers. Its repertoire is closely reminiscent of the motifs used in the decoration of carpets and ceramics, and betrays, once more, the Ottoman artists’ love of nature, their particular passion for flowers. 847012ff-11f1-5a0c-b2dd-0128cd68ab78.name: Textile fragment
847012ff-11f1-5a0c-b2dd-0128cd68ab78.description: This piece of cloth comes from a silk lampas fabric of which other fragments are in the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and Dallas Museum of Art (Keir Collection of Islamic Art), among other institutions. The fabric is decorated with the figures of turbaned hunters, some of them holding a bird in each hand, while others carry a gazelle in their arms. Woven in light-yellow and orange thread, the hunters stand out clearly against the black silk. Hunters wearing turbans are typical of the Safawid period (1501–1722/36) and also adorn contemporary miniatures.

The medallions contain palmettes, feathery leaves and naturalistic flowers, a combination regularly occurring on silks of the second half of the 16th century attributed to Istanbul. 8afba048-0957-5c1e-afda-b13a74187ad5.name: Cloth fragment.
8afba048-0957-5c1e-afda-b13a74187ad5.description:
The many different colours of the fragment combine serenely and harmoniously. The mainly red of beige background is decorated with strips containing geometric motifs (mostly medallions) alternating with floral patterns (stylised scrolled stalks and leaves) and highly stylised birds.  
The motifs are mainly in blue (indigo), yellow (saffron), and red (cochineal dye or lacquer). Beige-green and other colours accompany these.  
The cloth is woven in the manner used by Coptic weavers over several centuries. This fragment appears to come from high Egypt, well-known since ancient times for its weaving of wool.
8afba048-0957-5c1e-afda-b13a74187ad5.short_description: Fragment of a heavily dyed fabric combining geometric and plant motifs. The needlework techniques and decorative motifs are similar to those found in Egyptian *tiraz* from the Tulunid era. This fragment is thought to come from Upper Egypt, famed since Antiquity for its wool weaving.
8afba048-0957-5c1e-afda-b13a74187ad5.method_for_datation: The type of weaving and the decoration are similar to those found in Egyptian *tiraz* dating from the same Tulunid era in the 3rd / 9th century.

8c4076d1-62c9-5729-a3d5-d8c91345437b.name: Bridal headdress
8c4076d1-62c9-5729-a3d5-d8c91345437b.description: An example of coin-adorned accessories from Palestine dating to the early twentieth century, this bridal headdress originates from the villages of the Jaffa area. The coins incorporated into bridal ornaments symbolised part of the bride’s dowry, traditionally gifted by the groom’s family and considered her personal property, which she could keep and use according to her wishes. The embroidered motifs and techniques featured on the headdress are characteristic of the Jaffa region’s village dress traditions and are also found on women’s garments from the area.

8ef1e4eb-e7ca-506a-8117-7e5c9d0e9a18.name: Small Octagonal Pavilion Tent
8ef1e4eb-e7ca-506a-8117-7e5c9d0e9a18.short_description:
A tent comprising eight contiguous panels, each measuring 211cm x 135cm, and an octagonal canopy of eight triangular pieces. The plain-weave cotton exterior is embroidered with silk and metallic yarns, and the interior is lined with woven silk panels.  
The exterior of the tent is a plain-weave cotton, which is resistant to sunlight and less likely to be damaged by rain, while the interior is lined with more fragile and luxurious silk fabric. The form of this small pavilion tent inevitably recalls the shape of medieval Iranian octagonal tomb structures or gunbad, whose decorative brickwork frequently includes corner columns or "tent poles."  
One of the eight wall panels is designed to open as an entrance, and the central part of each wall panel is embellished by a fabric "grille" that clearly imitates Persian wooden or metal grille-work. The design provides plenty of shade and privacy coupled with maximum air circulation, and the door panel could be closed for additional privacy.

90f24fd2-747c-586e-b28c-441b69be0537.name: Textile fragment
90f24fd2-747c-586e-b28c-441b69be0537.description: This fragment of silk velvet came from the tent of Süleyman the Magnificent (1520–1566). The tent would have been seized by the sultan’s troops during one of the campaigns the Ottomans conducted in Persia from 1534 to 1554. Like the other fragments of the tent that have survived, it shows the refinement of the Persian textile arts in the 16th century, as well as their close links with miniatures. The execution of the figurative and floral motifs is highly accomplished. The design derives from the famous story of Khusraw and Shirin told in the poet Nizami’s *Khamsa* and illustrated in a great many miniatures. In that scene, Khusraw, who does not appear here, is usually shown with his finger to his lips in a gesture calling for silence. Another fragment of the tent is in the Keir Collection at the Dallas Museum of Art. The Montreal Museum of Fine Art’s fragment shows Shirin bathing, her clothing hung on the branches of a tree and her saddled horse nearby. Unlike the other surviving fragments, the inscription “amal Ghiyāth Al-Dīn Djāmī” on the saddle enables the piece to be attributed to the celebrated Safavid weaver Ghiyāth Al-Dīn Djāmī. According to Ackerman, Djāmī was not only a virtuoso weaver, but also one of the masters of the royal library. Eight other pieces attest to the fact that the weaver was active during the second half of the 16th century.

91ab6224-2ce2-5787-a444-869b675ead5e.name: Camel cover
91ab6224-2ce2-5787-a444-869b675ead5e.description: Because of their comparatively low weight, their durability, multifunctionality and their versatility in design, flatweaves and pile weavings were of great importance for a nomadic or semi-nomadic lifestyle. Large tent bags, throws, or hangings were prominently displayed, especially on treks. This kilim belongs to a group of pieces that were used as camel covers. When thrown over a loaded animal, the large-patterned sections hang down on either side, while the solid red centre section envelops the humps and back. The surface design, coloration and patterning of the piece are characteristic of southwestern Anatolia and refer to the Fethiye region. A full description of how such pieces were used and their design was illustrated in detail by Harald Böhmer in 2004 (English edition 2008). The Dresden piece is in excellent condition. It shows a clear, skilful pattern and colour design and appealing, well-balanced details, such as the bright, lateral line pattern separating the zigzag of the red background and blue border.

94a5375c-0f26-51bb-b2ed-85c5c6b0cf18.short_description: Used mostly to embellish garments, furnishings or household items, Islamic embroidery is also present on large textiles. The most important is *kiswa*, the cover enclosing the Ka'ba, which is sent every year to Mecca at the time of the pilgrimage. Over the door of the Ka'ba hangs an embroidery called *sitara*, decorated with inscriptions in different calligraphic styles. The present embroidery was probably destined to cover a mosque door. The rounded arch in the centre recalls the shape of the *mihrab* and its representation on prayer rugs. The entire surface of the cover, made from yellow, red, black, and turquoise pieces of silk, is decorated with cartouches and rosettes filled with vegetal and epigraphic motifs embroidered in the *dival* technique, i.e. over a base of paper or wool. The inscriptions, some of which were written in mirror-image, are illegible.

97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.name: Tapestry ‘after the Indian Manner’
97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.description: A tapestry with a number of colourful scenes and figure groups arranged on small islands decorated with exotic birds and flowering plants on a dark brown ground. These include a couple standing under a canopy holding by servants in the centre, two girls standing in front of a zig-zag fence with a parrot at the upper left, a small pagoda and a group of a sitting and a standing man in the upper right, two musicians, one with a drum and the other with beaters (the musical instrument is missing) in the lower foreground, and a monkey sitting on a palm tree at the lower right corner. The borders are composed of garlands of flowers and fruit arranged in Chinese pots in the lower border, linked with bunches of a silk ribbon in the upper border, decorated with candlesticks (?) in the right and the left sides and parrots and herons at the corners.

97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.method_for_provenance: John Vanderbank as the head of the Great Wardrobe workshop in London from 1689 to 1717, provided tapestries woven with ‘chinoiserie’ designs inspired by Chinese and Indian sources, lacquer panels, printed textiles etc. for Queen Mary’s apartments at Kensington Palace in 1690. Later he produced a second series with similar designs, but less elaborate figures, as cheaper versions for commercial sale. Numerous examples of Vanderbank's less elaborate series are known from the early 1700s – including, within the National Trust's collection, a small panel at Nunnington Hall in Yorkshire (no. 980694). – which is very close to this tapestry. Another, more similar item from the L. V. Hart collection was sold at Christie’s, November 12, 1964, no. 162, and November 29, 1979, no. 107. (Standen 1980, 126, fig. 10.), which depicts the same arrangement of the island panels, the couple under a canopy, the musicians, the ladies standing in front of a zig-zag fence, the pagoda, a monkey sitting on a palm tree and is framed by the same border-design.

9a5f6ab0-8a7b-5628-869a-8623164a2cfe.name: *Invasion of the French camp. The Swiss refuse to advance despite the interventions of their leaders*
9a5f6ab0-8a7b-5628-869a-8623164a2cfe.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
This tapestry depicts one of the decisive moments of the Battle of Pavia: the civilians are escaping from the French encampment, which is being attacked by the imperial troops, in the vicinity of the Vernavola river, through the breaches made in the wall of Visconti Park during the siege. The episode provides an opportunity to show everyday narratives: a soldier in the foreground runs away, carrying off with him a couple of chickens, while he looks towards the viewer, involving us in the scene; a woman in the distance carries a basket with two geese; a friar, frightened, is running. In the foreground, the Swiss infantry (recognisable by the flag with a white cross) who had fought with the French, proving their courage and valour, all hope of victory lost and surrounded on all sides, yield to the imperial cavalry, throwing their pikes to the ground, deaf to the cries of their officers, and try to seek safety in flight or surrender. In the foreground, amongst the soldiers one can make out a drummer, a piper and a standard bearer with a longsword, figures who often recur in military iconography. The figure in the centre of the tapestry has been identified as the Swiss captain Jean de Diesbach, who offers himself up to the sword of the enemy cavalier so he can die with honour (Casali 1993).

9afc3a98-4df9-5b49-8fc3-7de673068f6c.name: Embroidered linen.
9afc3a98-4df9-5b49-8fc3-7de673068f6c.description:
An embroidered textile thought to have served either as a cover for a divan (low sofa seat); a quilt facing; or as a hanging such as a curtain for a door. It is made up of three vertical lengths of linen sewn together and embroidered. The lattice design is inspired by AH 10th- and 11th- / AD 16th- and 17th-century silk textiles, and contains rows of palmettes made up of tulips and carnations, with the edges of the palmettes shaped in the form of serrated leaves. The silk-thread colours of red, green, blue and yellow are typical of the period; the stitch used is a regular darning stitch with the length of three counted threads over the linen, and one under it. Silk embroidery of the AH 11th- / AD 17th-century was a relatively cheap option for those who wanted to enjoy sumptuous textiles, given that woven-silk fabrics were much more expensive.  
  
It is sometimes difficult to distinguish between embroideries made by women at home and those worked by men in workshops for the trade. The pattern on this embroidery indicates that it was most probably made professionally in a workshop, because the composition relates strongly to similar designs found on woven-silk textiles of the time. This particular embroidery, unlike many similar to it in design, has no decorated border round its edges. This may suggest that it was used as a quilt facing. Quilts were backed with a sheet on one side; the edges of the sheet turned over the edge of the quilt, and lightly stitched on to the front where the quilt-facing would then be stitched too.

With no borders, this embroidery was most probably used as a quilt facing.

9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.name: Textile.
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.description: This large textile is embroidered on ivory-coloured organzine with lightweight pale-green silk satin (*atlas*) used as a base. The piece is particularly intricate and extremely refined, and most of it was needle-embroidered using silver-plated copper thread. The principal decorative motif is an ornate centre that resembles a prayer niche (*mihrab*), which is formed by a poly-lobed arch standing on two small columns, within which hangs a mosque lamp. A double rectangular cornice rounds off the decoration of the fabric. Its entire surface has been finely worked with a rich variety of motifs, including naturalistic vegetal motifs (flowers, leaves and small cypress trees) and epigraphic motifs. The repeated appearance of the *tughra*, the official monogram of the sultan as stamped on state documents, is of particular interest. Other inscriptions reproduce religious words and expressions relating to the Qur'an, both to ward off evil (‘*ana gelse red*’’ – ‘if difficulties arise, drive them away’) and for good omens (‘*el'an ba ' d-din*’ – ‘always with faith’). This fabric results from the manufacture of prayer mats (*seccade*) during the Ottoman era at the end of the AH 13th / AD 19th century. This piece may have been produced in Turkey or Egypt, although it was probably made in Ottoman Palestine.
9f93aaa3-18ce-5348-92f9-9826ae78f586.short_description: This sumptuously decorated fabric is a *seccade*, or prayer mat, finely decorated with naturalistic, plant and epigraphic motifs. It also includes the *tughra* (monogram) of Sultan Mustafa IV.

a319402b-f899-522c-a00d-0966b699e425.name: Cloth
a319402b-f899-522c-a00d-0966b699e425.short_description:
This devotional textile would hang from the ceiling or walls inside the Kaaba, the Muslim house of God in Mecca. Qur’anic verses in different calligraphy styles appear printed on red silk. Sultans would drape the Kaaba’s interior walls in silk from China or India as a religious offering since the Mamluk sultan al-Nassir Hassan in 1359.  
  
In medallions, *Tughra* calligraphy illustrates prayers and God’s names “the Merciful” and “the Generous”. The opening chapter of the Qur’an *al-Fatiha* and the *shahada* or declaration of faith rest between serrated lines in *thuluth* calligraphy.  
  
Protected from environmental factors inside the Kaaba, Muslim rulers would not change the interior silks annually but wash them twice a year. As a form of worship, the bestowal of this cloth would simultaneously achieve closeness to the shrine for blessings, reinforce the sanctity of the Kaaba and remind of the sultan’s power and prestige.

a4efc787-cbd4-5a26-bc2a-aa36772b6549.name: Tent.
a4efc787-cbd4-5a26-bc2a-aa36772b6549.description:
This tent belongs to the type of double-columned, rectangular tents with an oval floor plan. It consists of two rectangular walls, each of nine sections, and a roof. The two roof sections of the long sides and the triangular pieces of the short sides form a covering that resembles a vault. The tent roof and the walls are fastened to each other by a toggle and loop system. On the interior and exterior of the tent, this joint section is hidden by a valance. The lower edge of the tent wall also has a valance. The ceiling is supported by two columns. The wall sections do not have struts, but are made taut by guy ropes.  
The outer shell of the tent is of plain verdigris cloth. Only the inner shell of red cloth is decorated with a rich array of patterns. The composition and the motifs of this tent conform to general Ottoman tent ornamentation showing columns, arches, vases and medallions. A section of the wall was taken as a basic unit and its scheme of decoration was repeated on each of the other sections. The arches are filled with medallions called 'sun' (*şemse*). Each of the pointed medallions shows a great variety of flowers growing out from vase motifs. The dense floral infilling of the medallions and the borders presents the illusion of a garden. The arch and column motif likewise occurs on the ceiling of the tent. The ceiling with a band of star motifs between the two columns of the tent symbolises the sky.  
The ornamentation is worked in the hemmed appliqué technique. Pieces of silk fabric in various shapes and colours in combination with small pieces of leather were sewn to a ground to form patterns. It was carried out by placing a maximum of five layers of fabric on top of each other.  
The Swedes were never directly engaged in war against the Ottomans. Fighting against the Saxons, they captured a great deal of booty, also coming into ownership of Turkish tents.
a4efc787-cbd4-5a26-bc2a-aa36772b6549.short_description: Tent with an oval floor plan and two columns. The walls and roof are decorated with flowers and trees growing out of vases – the perfect illusion of a garden. In addition, the roof forming a vault shows a band of stars in the middle of the ceiling, symbolising the sky.
a4efc787-cbd4-5a26-bc2a-aa36772b6549.method_for_datation: The tent was captured from the Ottomans in 1683 following their failed siege of Vienna so it can be assumed that its date of manufacture was in the years before.
a4efc787-cbd4-5a26-bc2a-aa36772b6549.method_for_provenance: It was captured from the Turks. The tent shows traditional Ottoman form.
a4efc787-cbd4-5a26-bc2a-aa36772b6549.obtention: The tent came into the personal possession of the Swedish King Charles II in 1702. It was acquired by the Army Museum in 1898.

a5d9b0f5-29b8-59b7-a686-aa28e8c93f06.name: Cushion cover.
a5d9b0f5-29b8-59b7-a686-aa28e8c93f06.description: A hand-woven cushion cover of rectangular form that would have been used to back the low divans or sofas in Ottoman palaces from the AH 10th / AD 16th century onwards. The cushion is made of crimson-red voided velvet (a technique whereby the pile is cropped so short that the structure and colour of the field can be seen), and woven with green and cream threads. The composition is typical of the period, with a central field and two arched boarders; a large floral medallion fills the central field in this example. Having completed such a cover, the weaver did not cut it off the loom, but inserted a wooden baton between the Warp and the weft, and began on the next cover.
a5d9b0f5-29b8-59b7-a686-aa28e8c93f06.short_description: This cushion cover is made of a crimson-red voided velvet, where parts of its pile have been cropped very short so that the structure and colours of the warp and weft are exposed, creating an elaborate floral pattern. This type of velvet was sought after both within the Ottoman Empire and beyond.
a5d9b0f5-29b8-59b7-a686-aa28e8c93f06.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the elements of the pattern (a central field and two arched boarders; a large floral medallion in the central field) are a recurring theme in a variety of Turkish textiles and ceramics from the 10th / 16th century onwards.

a8fb3f11-1722-5b52-88a0-02f16ae87377.name: Suzani '*palak*'
a8fb3f11-1722-5b52-88a0-02f16ae87377.short_description:
“*Suzani*” or “*suzane*” derives from the Persian word "*suzan*" for "needle" and refers to bright silk embroidered wall hangings and bedspreads that adorned homes of people on festive occasions. The *suzani* culture developed in the ancient centres of agriculture and urban civilization of Central Asia (Turkestan) that for centuries served as points on international trade routes of the Great Silk Road.  
This is an excellent sample of an old Tashkent *suzani* called *palak*. This was the only kind of *suzani* where solar and astral motifs dominate over vegetative ones. According to ethnographical research data, big circles of the traditional *palak* pattern represent the moon and stars that were believed to provide good health and enhance female reproductive ability.  
The whole surface of the piece is entirely embroidered. Only natural dyes were used to colour the threads of the *suzani*. The dating of the item is supported by the bright hue of cochineal red dye, which was in use until the 1890s.

aa65e43b-2697-5ab6-8268-8bf7323bae3c.name: Qashqa´i kilim
aa65e43b-2697-5ab6-8268-8bf7323bae3c.description: In the 11th century, the Turkic peoples immigrated from Central Asia to Persia and probably lived first in northwestern Persia. It is unknown when the Qashqa´i moved to the southwest, but certainly at the latest when Turkmen conquered the Fars region in the middle of the 15th century. Many ethnic groups in southern and southwestern Persia, including several non-Turkmen, produced pile weavings and flatweaves. We have mainly come across works dating from the end of the 19th century to the first third of the 20th century. Due to confederations, pattern transfers and other considerations, it is not always possible to make a clear tribal attribution, especially with flatweaves. Some pieces are called "Qashqa´i" to indicate the outstanding quality of the work. The colour canon, pattern and shape, as well as material and fineness of this piece, suggest that it is a work of the Darashuri (sub-tribe of the Qashqa´i). The infinite repetition of colour-changing diamonds in free succession, often filled with diamonds and smaller cross shapes, appears both cheerful and unconstrained as well as powerfully determined. With its free, lively design, this flatweave is a characteristic example of a slit tapestry by southwestern Persia nomads.

aed82efb-32d2-5811-bb33-9c50bdadf8ac.name: Textile fragment
aed82efb-32d2-5811-bb33-9c50bdadf8ac.description: This fragment is an exceptional example of Buyid dynasty (945–1055) textiles from both a historical and an aesthetic viewpoint. The frieze is adorned with two-headed eagles carrying a winged creature and with stylized trees. The light-brown motifs are embellished with epigraphs that are particularly noticeable on the tops of the trees and on the band bordering the textile’s upper edge. The fragment’s style and iconography are similar to those of a group of four textiles discovered in the ancient necropolis of Nakhara Khanah, near Rayy. It remains to be determined whether this textile was designed to serve as a shroud or was selected from the belongings of the deceased.

b0fa7fe2-6439-5e4b-b775-f8024f171d3b.name: Military banner
b0fa7fe2-6439-5e4b-b775-f8024f171d3b.short_description:
This large banner was designed by the Ottoman calligrapher Sami Effendi (Hegira 1254–1330 / AD 1838–1912). It is inscribed with Qur’anic verses, praises of the Prophet Muhammad and his companions, proclamation of faith, and sayings. The inscription brocaded on the main field reflects the invocation used in war and combat. The signature of the calligrapher, Sami Effendi appears at the bottom right of this central rectangle panel, with an inscription that reads “Contentment is an everlasting treasure”.  
Sami Effendi’s father, Mahmud Effendi was the head of the quilt makers who was also involved in the preparation of banners and flags. The delicacy of the design reflects his experience and well deserved reputation as a renowned calligrapher. Large banner, or *sanjak*s, such as this was known to have been used to define the military districts of the Ottoman empire. They were mounted onto buildings or ships during expeditions, carried on poles during ceremonies and guarded well in war times.

b3b30c50-746b-58e7-9d2b-8bf0e782271e.name: Tiraz Textile
b3b30c50-746b-58e7-9d2b-8bf0e782271e.short_description: This linen textile with its regal purple inscription naming the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir has lost much of it original length due to its use as a burial shroud. However, it preserves almost its full width, spanned by the decorative inscription band. Known as a “*tiraz*” textile, it is unusually wide and was perhaps a shawl. The term “*tiraz*” actually means “embroidery,” but came to denote an inscription band as one sees on these textiles and on anything else, including architecture. Most of the medieval textiles discovered in excavations in Egypt had been used as burial shrouds and have suffered similar deterioration. Only those that found their way into European church treasuries are well preserved and give us an idea of how the full garment appeared. *Tiraz* textiles, despite their Arabic inscriptions, were highly valued in Europe as relics of the Holy Land and appear as the costumes of Christ and the Virgin in Italian Renaissance paintings.

b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.name: Fragment of woven linen.
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.description:
A textile fragment of plain-woven linen with tapestry-woven decorative bands executed in silk, the pattern comprising three horizontal, superposed decorative bands, each separated by areas of plain weaving. The uppermost band, flanked by golden scrolling borders with red outlines and blue detailing, contains a zigzag band with a simple scroll outlined in red on a golden ground. Blue trident-like motifs fill the remaining spaces above and below the zigzag pattern. Below this is a slightly narrower decorative stripe that has a cursive inscription set against a deep-red background, flanked by stylised split-palmette borders above and below. The third and narrowest band has a central wavy green strip on a gold background, and two gold palmette-scroll borders set on a red ground.  
  
This textile fragment is a good example of the artistic influence that the Coptic communities who settled in Egypt had on textile production during the Fatimid period. There remains to this day a sizeable Coptic population in Egypt.
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.short_description: Islamic Egypt was famed for the production of sophisticated wool, linen and silk textiles made in specialist workshops. These were manned by Coptic Christian textile workers as well as Muslims. This textile was collected by Henry Wallis (1830–1916), a famous painter and expert on Middle Eastern ceramics.
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.type: Fatimid textile, woven linen, tapestry silk
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.method_for_datation: This textile has been tentatively dated to the 6th/12th century on the basis of general similarities with other textiles of the Fatimid period.
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that textile fragments with this type of decoration and epigraphic detail were produced in Fatimid Egypt. This is due to so many having been found in burials and excavations throughout Upper Egypt in particular.
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.provenance: From a tomb at al-Drounka, Egypt.
b6c68555-4721-5c09-8439-5598ae6f7fdd.obtention: This textile together with several other Fatimid textile fragments were acquired by NMS in 1898 from Henry Wallis, a famous Pre-Raphaelite painter, who travelled and painted extensively in Egypt and elsewhere. Subsequently he became a highly respected expert on Egyptian and Persian ceramics.

b7f46ff9-52a1-5495-80f5-c075d3bfc0da.name: *Defeat of the French cavalry. The imperial infantry seize the enemy’s artillery*
b7f46ff9-52a1-5495-80f5-c075d3bfc0da.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the right-hand border of the fabric; this mark can also be observed on another tapestry in the series. The presence of the weaver’s mark has also allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: between 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here should be read in close continuity with the subject represented in *Advance of the imperial troops*. In fact, by juxtaposing the two tapestries one can reconstruct, as C. Paredes suggests, the landscape and the troop movements on the battlefield. In particular, in the foreground one can recognise the group of imperial arquebusiers, led by their commander, Fernando Francesco d’Avalos, who is identified by the letters “MAR. DE PES” (an abbreviation of “Marquis of Pescara”) on the neck of his horse. In the centre, further writing, “MARQ.IS DU VASTE”, indicates the presence on the battlefield of Alfonso d’Avalos, Marquis of Vasto. On the right is depicted the ferocious battle between the imperial landsknechts, led by Georg von Frundsberg, distinguished by their white and red sashes, and the mercenary troops of the “Banda Nera”, in the service of the French. Noting the detail of the capture of the French artillery in the panoramic overview extending into the preceding tapestry, as mentioned above, it is possible to discern that the French canons have stopped firing to avoid striking the back of their King, who, breaking through the ranks, throws himself at the enemy, just as sources describe.  
This tapestry, along with three others in the series, still has its original border, with decorative motifs in which flowers, fruit, birds and animals are depicted. However, according to a description from the 1770s, the lower borders originally introduced decorative motifs with tritons and sea horses, similar to those that appear in the *Hunts of Maximilian*, another series of tapestries produced for Charles V by the same workshop from designs by van Orley, and today in the Louvre. Hence, the entire lower strip, detached some time after the 1770s and subsequently reassembled, appears to have been re-sewn using parts of the borders of other tapestries, which now are missing them, and which were originally intended to adorn the vertical edge of the fabric (Buchanan 2002).

bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.name: Painted wall-hanging: The Day of Judgement (*Ruz-e mahshar*)
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.short_description: A painted wall-hanging depicts the *Day of Judgement* from a Shi'ite perspective in Isfahan. The main theme is the reward given in paradise to the martyrs who fell at Kerbala on 10 October 680, corresponding to the Islamic date 10 Muharram 61, and the agonies of their enemies on Judgement Day. Elements of Christian iconography are present. There is the trumpeting angel who blows into the bugle at the Last Judgement; the receiving of the arisen into heaven; the two angels who attend to the weighing scale of the souls; the chosen ones who await their entry into paradise; the blood witnesses who in advance enjoy the delights of paradise; and finally those of different faiths and traitors, who, already condemned, stand before the infernal ground. There are also new elements: the prophet of Islam is now an established, important figure, and Christ, the judge of the world, assumes the part of a precursor-prophet.

bcb08e82-a842-5d85-bc9a-00e84a746ec1.name: Dragon Sileh (Zili) rug or Verneh (Varni) Cover
bcb08e82-a842-5d85-bc9a-00e84a746ec1.description: This rug, originally intended as a cover, was woven in two pieces and sewn together in the middle. Also known as "Dragon Zili" rugs, these carpets were mainly woven in the Jabrail District of Artsak (Nagorno-Karabagh), using the soumak technique. Their characteristic pattern consists of stylized dragons in the shape of an "S" aligned in horizontal and vertical rows. The colour of the dragon alternates; their bodies are filled with tinier "S" motifs; the spaces in between with human, animal, and geometric patterns. In Azerbaijan and Russian literature, such items are called *Verneh* (Varni) covers. Its speciality lies in the fact that the direction of the "S"-shaped dragons in the bottom row of the right side is opposite the rest.

bf169ede-be12-53cb-9b5e-3959e1451970.name: Tent hanging.
bf169ede-be12-53cb-9b5e-3959e1451970.description:
This long, narrow, silk textile consists of a central field with a border. The central field shows a loosely conceived lattice composed of interconnected tulips, four of which face towards an eight-petalled rosette at every junction of the lattice. The spaces created by the lattice contain eight-pointed-star motifs; these in turn contain a central roundel enclosing an eight-petalled rosette with green trefoils and red serrated leaves, which extend outwards from the border of the roundels. The whole composition of the central field is set against a deep crimson background. The outer border consists of an inner and outer band with floral scrolling that encloses a central area enhanced by an intricate arabesque scroll.  
Tent hangings such as this one were used to adorn the interior ‘walls’ of tents used by royalty or high officials when they were away from their urban palaces.
bf169ede-be12-53cb-9b5e-3959e1451970.short_description: This silk tent panel, with its floral lattice design of tulip heads and rosettes enclosing central star motifs recalling imperial Ottoman textiles, is attributed to Syria on the basis of stylistic similarities with contemporary artefacts and textiles made in that important Ottoman province.
bf169ede-be12-53cb-9b5e-3959e1451970.method_for_datation: The piece has been dated to the 11th / late 16th or early 17th century on the basis of stylistic comparison with contemporary artifacts and textiles from Ottoman Turkey and Syria.

bfdbe8a5-e335-5014-a461-8cecc5b16445.name: A complete cover for a Damascus *mahmal*, with the name of Sultan Mehmed IV
bfdbe8a5-e335-5014-a461-8cecc5b16445.short_description:
The *mahmal* was a ceremonial palanquin that represented the authority of the Sultan over the Holy Places. The Mamluk sultan Baybars (r. 1260 – 1277) is reported to be the first to have sent a mahmal with the caravan of pilgrims from Cairo, and the custom was continued under Ottoman rule and almost without interruption until the early 20th century. This, the earliest of seven mahmal covers in the Khalili Collections, is an example of a second mahmal which left Damascus with the caravan of Syrian and Turkish pilgrims. The Egyptian and Syrian mahmals were occasionally joined by a third mahmal from the Yemen.  
  
The embroidered Qur’anic verses are apposite: the text on the pyramid top is Qur’an, *sura* *al-Ahzab* (XXXIII), verse 56, which mentions the Prophet; the band around the lower part has al-Baqara (II) verse 127, which refers to Abrahim and Isma‘il raising the foundations of the House, that is, the Ka‘ba. At the very top, below the finial, is *sura* *al-Nahl* (XVI), verse 7: ‘And they carry your heavy loads to lands that you could not otherwise reach except with souls distressed’.

c0c780b7-bc1e-5c06-ace4-ef7fefd9fa80.description: This wool fragment from the Umayyad dynasty (AD 661–750) is adorned with a medallion depicting an eagle in shades of blue, green and yellow. The inside of the medallion’s dark-green border is dotted with 20 scrolls, while another series of scrolls topped by floral designs provides its outline. Geometric and plant motifs are visible in the corners. Ecru scrolls, topped in their case by red and orange flowers, figure on the main border, which has a brown ground. A wide band of ecru is enhanced by a rectangle with red, green and yellow geometric patterns. Here the floral designs consist of palmettes and rosettes. The depiction of medallions embellished with figures is derived from Persian silks; the decorative motifs within such medallions are characteristic of Sasanian decorative arts.

c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.name: Tablecloth (*dastarkhan*)
c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.description:
A *dastarkhan* is a thin white *palas* (a kind of traditional, flat-woven carpet popular in Azerbaijan) that functioned as a tablecloth for Azerbaijanis and other Turkic peoples. The central field of Azerbaijani *dastarkhans* was rectangular, usually plain, and the borders spotted vivid decoration in contrast with the *dastarkhans* produced in Central Asia that boast elaborate designs. A *dastarkhan* denoted a sacred meaning, as its ornaments protected the food and the breadwinner and brought abundance to the family.  
In the central field of this artifact, there are inscriptions in the old epigraphic alphabet, stylized images of birds (symbolizing protection), butas (symbolizing different abilities bestowed on a person) and branches (symbolizing blessings). Images of arrows on the *dastarkhan's* border symbolize honour, prosperity and blessings.

c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.name: Flag of a workers’ league bearing the sign
c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.short_description:
This flag presumably belonged to a league of navvies, or labourers. It shows the tools used by workers employed in road construction, i.e. pickaxe and shovel.  
Starting from the last decades of the XIX century, trade unionism flourished in Italy. In the 1890s, in many towns different unions started to reunite in general unions at a town level, known as Camere del Lavoro (labour unions, modelled on the French Bourse du Travail). In 1906 the Confederazione Generale del Lavoro (CGdL), a national confederation of trade unions, was founded.

c166cd2d-8939-540b-a898-6cea4e8dc0ae.short_description: Figurative design flowered in Safavid textiles in the AH 10th century / AD mid-16th century. c23d10a7-1e62-576e-94be-aa1878e96194.name: Cushion cover '*çatma yastık*'
c23d10a7-1e62-576e-94be-aa1878e96194.short_description:
This is "*çatma yastık yüzü*" - a luxurious cushion cover of voided and brocaded velvet used to embellish salons of rich houses in the Ottoman Empire of the AD 16th–mid 18th centuries.  
For nearly 150 years the shape (rectangular, about 110cm x 60 cm) and the basic design of *çatma yastik* covers remained unchanged. The ornamented central field is flanked with two borders, each consisting of six arched cartouches filled with smaller floral motifs.  
The museum piece featuring large “*çintamani*” circles as a central motif was most likely produced in the period of the late 16th–first half of the 17th centuries. The high quality of silk, the deep crimson tone and the lavish application of silver wrapped thread (now partly lost) - all indicate that the cushion cover was made in Bursa, the key centre of the Ottoman silk weaving industry.

c27af56e-a4e0-51fb-a73b-60b44f2b7999.name: Tomb cover.
c27af56e-a4e0-51fb-a73b-60b44f2b7999.description: A section of red silk divided into ivory-coloured zigzag bands. These bands form a three-part repeat unit in which the main section is a wide band containing the Muslim profession of faith, the Shahada. Above this, a border band contains a verse from the Qur'an (2: 144) which concerns the *qibla*, or direction of prayer. Below, a pious invocation reads 'Praise God and glorify Him; praise God the mighty.' These repeat units are separated by bands in which finial-shaped pendants, facing alternately up and down, are arranged among circular medallions; these shapes contain rhyming invocations: 'O Benefactor (ya mannan)!' and 'O Compassionate (ya hannan)!' in the pendants, and 'O Praise (ya subhan)!' and 'O Authority (ya sultan)!' in the circles. Textiles like this one were made under the Ottomans to cover the cenotaphs of important individuals. Since the deceased is buried facing Mecca, the inclusion of the Qur'anic verse about the *qibla* has special significance. This particular type of tomb cover appears to have been woven in large quantities, as silks with an identical pattern can be found in collections all over the world.
c27af56e-a4e0-51fb-a73b-60b44f2b7999.short_description: A section of red silk woven with zigzag bands containing several repeating inscriptions, among them Qur’anic verses and rhyming invocations of God. Many similar textiles were made under the Ottomans as tomb covers and as linings for the Ka’ba in Mecca.

c791fd67-b769-5838-8662-48cd1f3c7839.name: *Mafrash* (Bedding Bag) End Panel
c791fd67-b769-5838-8662-48cd1f3c7839.description:
Certain textiles from Anatolia, covers and containers made by nomads, semi-nomads and villagers for their own use known as the Caucasus and Iran, first came to the attention of consumers in Europe, in the final third of the 19th century. Although the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts purchased its first nomad and village flat-woven textiles at the turn of the 19th/20th century, this carpet was a donation by Prof. Ottó Fettick (1946, followed by his bequest in 1954) that laid the real foundations of the Museum's woven carpet collection. The 104 items included textiles of a kind that were new to the Museum: 19th-century woven Caucasian and North Iranian soumak, palas, verneh and jajim rugs, containers and covers, and Anatolian, Iranian and Balkan kilims. Professor Fettick (1875–1954) was a veterinary surgeon, bacteriologist and art collector and probably started building his collection of 19th-century flat-woven nomad carpets and other textiles in the early 20th century. The end panel of a Shahsevan *mafrash* (bedding bag) presumably from the Moghan-Savalan region is from the Fettick collection. Its ornament is comprised of three broad horizontal bands. The dark brown central band has offset rows of hooked hexagons; one row in alternating colours between two rows of white half hexagons. The upper and lower secondary broad bands contain right-facing peacocks standing in line on a yellow ground, each with a stylized "cock" motif on its back.  
  
Originally the side panel selvedges were sewn together with a blue and brown rope-like overcasting which remained on three edges of the end panel when the *mafrash* was taken apart. The cut edge of the long side panel is visible on the lower third of the left side under the frayed overcasting.  
  
There is a *mafrash* end panel of almost identical pattern in the Charles Grant Ellis Collection.

c88cfa39-a575-5369-b26b-986d4b8b0529.name: Two embroidered tent panels
c88cfa39-a575-5369-b26b-986d4b8b0529.short_description: The panels were apparently used to cover the entrance of a Persian tent made in the Caspian city of Rasht, famous for its embroideries. The lush composition, laid out symmetrically along the central axis of the entrance, recalls the designs of the so-called ‘meditation rugs’. It includes, at the centre of a large polylobed arch, the crown of a cypress tree, and, at the foot of the tree, on both sides, a lion holding a sword – symbol of ‘Ali, and a peacock – symbol of paradise. The panels feature an allover design of floral motifs and birds embroidered in chain stitch. An outer border embroidered with *boteh* (paisley) motifs on a red ground encloses the panels on three sides.

c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.name: Fragment of woven linen and silk.
c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.description: A woven linen and silk slit-tapestry fragment in cream, golden yellow, crimson and blue. The design consists of three superposed bands, the uppermost and the lowest identical in appearance. The design is tripartite, with two bands of *naskhi* script rendered in red on a gold background, and flanking a gold-coloured central guilloche band outlined in red with gold-coloured rabbit-like motifs in the centre of every loop. Narrow stripes with wavy patterning complete the pattern. The inscriptions in the epigraphic panels read: *‘… wa al-iqbal’* (‘… and prosperity’). In between these two bands is a broader panel with a complex, gathered linear interlaced design in gold and red which employs individual gold-coloured rabbit-like motifs set against a red ground.
c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.short_description: Fatimid Egypt was famous for the production of sophisticated silk textiles produced in court-sponsored workshops known as ‘*tiraz*’ workshops. Most were fashioned into royal garments for the sultan and his court or robes of honour to be bestowed on worthy courtiers, dignitaries or foreign diplomats.
c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.type: Fatimid textile woven linen and silk
c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.dates: Hegira 570–96 / AD third quarter of the 12th century.
c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.method_for_datation: The decorative style of this textile fragment places it within the category of very late Fatimid textiles, characterized by the exclusive use of golden yellow and red, together with the complexity of the interlace designs which covers the central band completely. The inscription in *naskhi* script also helps to place the production of this piece within the reign of the last Fatimid rulers. Furthermore this item has been dated on the basis of its striking similarity to a linen and silk fragment in the Bouvier Collection in Geneva, which is dated 570–96 / third quarter of the 12th century.
c9e57bf4-504f-5953-928e-e4f5dacd9861.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that textile fragments with this type of decoration and epigraphic detail were produced in Fatimid Egypt. This is due to so many having been found in burials and excavations throughout Upper Egypt in particular.

cb646540-71b4-53fd-9b5d-065a402f6c3b.name: 'Hortus Conclusus' church tapestry
cb646540-71b4-53fd-9b5d-065a402f6c3b.description: In our time, people who want to improve their logic skills might do a Sudoku while commuting on the urban railway. In medieval times, people would spend their time decoding the immense iconographic programme of the Catholic Church, which included not only Biblical figures and saints, but also legendary creatures with no religious connotations. The creator of the “Enclosed Garden” that can be seen on a precious tapestry from the chapel of Ried in what is today the canton of Schwyz drew on the early Christian natural history treatise known as the Physiologus, which states that a unicorn can only be captured by a virgin. From a Christian viewpoint, the virgin is Mary and her touching the unicorn’s horn is an allusion to the immaculate conception. Interpreting this scene correctly was tricky, but within the capabilities of medieval churchgoers. In contrast, they were less adept at understanding written letters and numbers.

cba9697e-4726-5cc0-9a64-80be790a931d.name: Fragment of an interior Kiswa Cover for the Ka'ba in Makkah
cba9697e-4726-5cc0-9a64-80be790a931d.short_description: For four hundred years, the Ottomans sent money and gifts to Makkah and Medina with the Surre procession. The gifts included covers for the Ka’ba, made in Cairo and Istanbul, which were replaced every year. Old covers were returned to the palace in Istanbul, distributed to the faithful or sometimes reused.Textiles like this one were made in Istanbul and Bursa from the 10th century H/ 16th century to the early 14th century H/ 20th century. Woven in red and beige silk, they were intended for draping either the inner walls of the Ka’bah in Makkah or those of the Tomb of the Prophet in Madina. Their zig-zag design echoes that of the main kiswa but the religious inscriptions vary according to the textiles’ intended use. Here, the combination of texts with their emphasis on the Prophet suggests that this fragment was part of a hanging intended for the Prophet’s tomb chamber, which also houses the cenotaphs of his first two successors, the caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar ibn al Khattab.

ce91431e-97e8-5a65-8d88-f4d8be6111e9.short_description: The large linen fragment has two lines of inscriptions running in opposite directions and woven in dark blue silk thread. The content of the text, in the *kufic* script, follows the typical form for *tiraz* textiles conveying good wishes to the caliph Nizar Abu al-Mansur al-imam al-Aziz and states that it was woven in the royal *tiraz* workshop of Tinnis in the year 3(7)5.

d0d2ab0e-7d90-5e08-89b9-cfab8bae0d85.name: Section from the *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba
d0d2ab0e-7d90-5e08-89b9-cfab8bae0d85.short_description:
The pattern consists of zigzag bands alternately enclosing the *shahada* (‘There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God’) and the invocation ‘O! God, May his Majesty be exalted’, the latter in mirrored script. It is possible that the calligraphy was designed by the master calligrapher, ‘Abdallah Zuhdi, who was known as *katib al-haramayn* (‘the calligrapher of the two holy sanctuaries’).  
Egypt had been supplying the *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba on a yearly basis, and almost without interruption, since Fatimid times. Since the early 1970s, however, the *kiswa* has been woven in a special workshop in Mecca.

d0d6c9d5-6ebd-5af5-9fa7-3367e09d88aa.name: Curtain for the door of the Ka‘ba, with the name of Sultan Ahmed I
d0d6c9d5-6ebd-5af5-9fa7-3367e09d88aa.short_description:
In her study of the Ka‘ba door curtains in the Topkapı Sarayı, Hülya Tezcan has identified four main styles. The earliest is that of a curtain bearing the name of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent and the date AH 950 / AD 1543–4. The second style, to which this curtain belongs, apepars to have been popular for a long period, as known examples date from the late 16th to the late 18th century.  
  
Characteristic features of this style include the five arches at the top, as well as the zigzag panels and the reciprocal ogival cartouches at the bottom. The commisioning order and date are in the two panels immediately above the latter. This curtain was commisioned and presented to the Ka‘ba by Sultan Ahmed I.

d1baf7da-b838-5564-a184-03f1f16c1457.name: Fragment of woven linen.
d1baf7da-b838-5564-a184-03f1f16c1457.description: A fragment with two superposed decorative bands separated from each other by an area of plain weave. Both bands are identical in design: guilloches rendered in a yellowish gold colour, set against a blue background. The central areas of the guilloche’s loops have light-coloured palmette-leaves in them, which are set against either a red or black background. The guilloche band of is flanked above and below by two red stripes, each containing a light-coloured *kufic* inscription enhanced by regularly disposed, gold-coloured scrolling motifs; the outer borders of these are formed by a system of interlocking wave-like designs. The inscription has been deciphered as: ‘victory comes from God’. Akhmim in Egypt lies on the east bank of the River Nile. The linen-weaving industry was an important one there, and textiles and handicrafts are still produced in Akhmim today.
d1baf7da-b838-5564-a184-03f1f16c1457.short_description: Many Fatimid and Mamluk textiles have been found in burials around Akhmim, an important Egyptian textile centre with a famous linen-weaving industry. Interestingly, the history of Akhmim is closely linked with that of the Coptic community in Egypt and retains a sizeable Coptic population to this day.
d1baf7da-b838-5564-a184-03f1f16c1457.type: Fatimid textile, woven linen and silk
d1baf7da-b838-5564-a184-03f1f16c1457.method_for_datation: A fragment in the Bouvier Collection in Geneva bears a close stylistic resemblance with this piece and it has been dated to the late 5th–early 6th / first half of the 12th century.

d1d438f0-83d2-5fda-b51d-574d3965aaa9.name: Silk textile with geometric pattern.
d1d438f0-83d2-5fda-b51d-574d3965aaa9.description: A silk textile with a lampas weave, satin ground and weft-faced tabby pattern. Yellow strap-work bands on a red background create a dazzling geometric interlace design in which eight-pointed stars figure prominently. Other colours, such as pink, green, and a silvery blue, are used to create contrasts and highlights. Textiles like this one were made in the Nasrid period in southern Spain and North Africa. They continued to be valued throughout Europe long after the fall of the Nasrid dynasty; this particular example was hanging behind a statue of the Virgin Mary in Florence, Italy as late as the 19th century.
d1d438f0-83d2-5fda-b51d-574d3965aaa9.short_description: A silk textile woven with an elaborate geometric pattern based on eight-pointed stars. Textiles like this were woven in southern Spain and North Africa during the Nasrid period. This example may have served as a hanging to enliven an architectural setting.

d3cbf39d-5c09-5ef2-9a4f-78a92ddbb910.name: Ikat hanging
d3cbf39d-5c09-5ef2-9a4f-78a92ddbb910.short_description:
The decoration of this wall hanging has been achieved through the ikat technique, and depicts one of the most popular décors of the Qajar period: cypresses in a niche. Further to this, in this particular example another popular motif, the peacock, has been added to the tips of the small cypresses. Comparable wall hangings made of silk ikat have survived mainly from Yazd, hence its likely provenance.  
  
Ikat weavings appeared sporadically in Iran as early as the 17th and 18th centuries, but remained the great exception. In the 19th century, especially in the second half, ikat weaving flourished, experiencing a period of artistic development. During this period, the ever increasing imports of cheap European machine-made goods posed enormous problems for local textile manufacturers. However, the ikat weavers were able to successfully hold their own against the competition.

d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.name: Pearl Diver’s Finger Protectors
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.short_description: These finger guards are known as khabt (pl. khabta). They were an essential part of a pearl-diver's equipment, as they protected his finger tips from the sharp oyster shells and other unexpected dangerous objects the pearl-diver might brush his fingers against while searching the murky seabed. Much of his work had to rely on touch, as visibility was minimal and few dangers could be anticipated by sight alone. When not used, the finger guards were kept in a container filled with water to keep them supple.

d5063c4c-2fb6-5145-80ab-45cf9cbda6d3.name: Section from the *kiswa* of the Prophet’s tomb
d5063c4c-2fb6-5145-80ab-45cf9cbda6d3.short_description:
This section from a *kiswa* of the Prophet’s tomb belongs to a small group of fragments in which the finely calligraphed *thuluth* inscriptions are woven in silver-wrapped silk thread on a deep raspberry-pink ground. Selin Ipek has suggested that, given the amount of silver used in its weaving, the *kiswa* from which they come must have been a special commission.  
  
The vertical repeat consists of four wide zigzag bands alternating with four narrower ones; there are two horizontal repeats per loom width. The first wide band at the top of the textile has a supplication to God for blessings and peace upon Prophet. In the narrow band below that is *sura al-Ikhlas* (CXII), followed by the *shahada* in the wide band. Next is *sura al-Ahzab* (XXXIII), verse 56. The third wide band has *Allahu wala siwahu* (‘God and there is none equal to Him’), with a small flower under each of the words, Allah. Inscribed in the last narrow band in the repeat is *sura al-Qasas* (XXVIII), end of verse 88.

d588c3c2-379b-534f-8feb-9c9bc83a8d5c.name: Two sections from a tomb cover
d588c3c2-379b-534f-8feb-9c9bc83a8d5c.short_description:
The calligraphic design on each of these two sections consists of an eight-fold repeat of Qur’an, *sura* *al-Fath*, XLVIII, verse 1: *inna fatahna laka fathan mubinan*. The letters have been manipulated to create the semblance of a cartouche in which the words *inna fatahna* and *laka fathan* – which are similar in form – have been arranged at either end to suggest a mirror image around the word *mubinan* in the centre.  
A similar textile in the Musée Historique des Tissus, Lyon, France, bears the date AH 1123 (AD 1711–12).

d5ef573d-2a05-5d47-a3e9-ad45caf58169.name: Flag of the St Petersburg Colony of Macedonians
d5ef573d-2a05-5d47-a3e9-ad45caf58169.short_description: This flag was the symbol of the St. Petersburg Colony of Macedonians, a group of Macedonian intellectuals who lived and worked in St. Petersburg and shared the same ideas and interests – working for the liberation and recognition of Macedonia. The red colour of the flag symbolizes the blood shed in the centuries-long Macedonian struggle for autonomy. The white rectangle in the upper left corner bears a depiction of a unicorn, also in red colour.

d7096975-0651-52ea-8630-a12bafecd7a2.short_description: This black-blue fragment of shawl is decorated with tapestry bands woven with *kufic* inscriptions and highly stylized human figures, quadrupeds and birds. The overall stylization is reminiscent of Coptic textiles but is typical of the Fayyum area in Upper Egypt, which is attested by Muslim writers as specializing in the weaving of woollen fabrics.

e02118f9-dc4c-59ac-97f3-1e1641712dd1.name: Fragmentary loom width with wavy-vine pattern
e02118f9-dc4c-59ac-97f3-1e1641712dd1.short_description: Spectacular silks with large scale patterns were favoured materials for luxury garments among the courtly elite of sixteenth-century Istanbul and were often used for the bold, richly coloured kaftans of the Ottoman sultans. In this example, the vertical pattern of foliage is stylistically similar to that of the ceramic wall tiles in buildings of the period. The weave, referred to in Turkish as *kemha*, incorporates metal-wrapped thread into a lampas, or multiweave fabric. Ottoman *kemha* fabrics typically combine a satin ground with a woven twill design highlighted with gold. Their glittering patterns catch the light and appear to float above a shimmering background.

e2301ec1-c5b6-5d83-a402-0bf32d43fab0.name: Section from the belt of the Ka‘ba
e2301ec1-c5b6-5d83-a402-0bf32d43fab0.short_description:
The *hizam* (‘belt’) is an inscribed band that encircles the upper part of the Ka‘ba. During the Ottoman period, it was made up of eight sections – two on each wall – and this section would have been on the south side. It is embroidered with *sura al-‘Imran* (III), verses 95–97. The text refers to ‘the religion of Abraham’; ‘the first house of worship that was in Mecca’; and ‘the Station of Abraham’.  
The *kiswa* and its various components had been supplied yearly, and with very few exceptions, since Fatimid times. An incident at Mina during the Hajj of 1926 led to a break in the relation between Egypt and Saudi Arabia. As the season of Hajj approached the following year, and with no *kiswa* arriving from Egypt, King ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Saud ordered one to be made in haste at Dar al-Kiswa in Mecca. Due to the shortness of time, the *hizam*, of which this is a section, had to be machine-embroidered.

e4957137-fe26-5b45-a98b-c7918535c481.name: Textile fragment
e4957137-fe26-5b45-a98b-c7918535c481.description: Textiles constitute a major part of the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts’ collection of Islamic art. The decorative arts had great symbolic and social importance in the Islamic world. The skills of the weavers of the time have rarely been equalled, and this fragment is among the pieces that demonstrate the complexity and innovation of their techniques. Figurative designs, which were extremely popular in 16th-century Persia, appeared on garments and palace furnishings, as well as in religious and funeral ceremonies. In this fragment of reversible double cloth depicting “Boats at Sea”, two fabrics have been produced simultaneously, one over the other, following a repeat pattern of remarkable detail: sailing boats with four sailors alternating with simple rowing boats carrying three figures, all on a sea filled with fish and ducks. The vertical masts create the impression of stability, while the diagonal placement of the rowing boats suggests a rocking motion. The red motifs lay on a silver-thread ground.
e4957137-fe26-5b45-a98b-c7918535c481.method_for_datation: Stylistic and comparative analyses; *Catalogue of the International Exhibition of Persian Art*, London: Royal Academy, 1931, cat. no. 301a.

e5229f07-7f0c-5c3d-b332-abfb11f167a3.name: Fragmentary silk velvet with repeating tiger-stripe and *çintamani* design
e5229f07-7f0c-5c3d-b332-abfb11f167a3.short_description:
This early example of *çintamani* silk velvet incorporates the triangular formation of three circles alternating with two wavy bands. This pattern, whose name is derived from a Sanskit term meaning “auspicious jewel”, appears on Ottoman textiles, carpets, and ceramics  
The pile in luxurious textiles like this one is created by the warp threads, which are looped during the weaving process and then sheared to create a plush surface. Polychromatic designs were formed by alternating two or more warps in contrasting colours, and brocaded with metal-wrapped weft threads creating the "voided" ground in the design.

e6f5f348-ba35-50e4-9c8e-f3ed312366b0.name: Embroidery.
e6f5f348-ba35-50e4-9c8e-f3ed312366b0.description: An embroidery comprising rows of stylised red tulips and blue palmette heads, arranged in ascending order, alternating each other on undulating black stems and detailed with pink-peach and three shades of green. Being a highly sophisticated piece, this embroidery shows a crisp, well-executed drawing technique and vigorous movement and elasticity in its design. Many such types of embroidery were influenced by the brocades and velvets that were designed and made for the Ottoman court; these include a well-defined group of brocades with undulating stems, which must have influenced the layout of this embroidery.
e6f5f348-ba35-50e4-9c8e-f3ed312366b0.short_description: Many such Turkish Ottoman embroideries were influenced by the brocades and velvets that were designed and made for the Ottoman court; these include a well-defined group with undulating stems, which must have influenced the layout of this one, with its fantastic tulip and palmette heads.
e6f5f348-ba35-50e4-9c8e-f3ed312366b0.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the depiction of Tulips in this style is typical of Turkish Ottoman art. These Tulips appear on nearly all types of materials, including ceramics, miniature paintings, and a variety of woven fabrics as well as embroideries, from the 10th / 16th century onwards.

e8eaafdf-a77c-51a2-8c54-e52092c06b0b.short_description:
Silk *limar* cloth; predominantly blue & red. eb5b519d-c67d-5a80-8e09-395571ae29b1.name: Embroidery.
eb5b519d-c67d-5a80-8e09-395571ae29b1.description:
The nearly square textile with fringed ribbon shows all-over silver and gold embroidery. In spite of its complexity and density, the structure of the symmetrically composed design is evident. In the middle appears a *tughra*, the monogram of the Ottoman sultans, surrounded by four slightly curved flower sprays forming a small circle. The remaining area is dedicated to a motif repeated in the four corners. This motif shows a rococo-inspired basket edged with and flanked by scrolled leafy sprays on a small console and with a bouquet in it. Worked in a metal thread of a different hue, the pairs of birds beside the bouquets and all the large and small blossoms and flower sprays filling the area between are arranged in a circle.  
To judge from the perfect composition of the design and the high technical quality it is professional embroidery by an urban workshop. But there is another clue too. This design composed of a small inner circle formed by the *tughra* and a large outer circle suggests that the textile was used as a turban cover. To keep dust off a turban a special, always square, cover was introduced indicating its particular purpose by a circle set in the middle. However, this cover differs from the usual scheme of an inner circle design repeated in the outer one because of its manufacture for Palace use. Pieces showing a *tughra* on them were primarily made for the Palace. The *tughra* in this embroidery has been simplified and distorted, but it might be that of Sultan 'Abd al-'Aziz (Abdülaziz in Turkish).
eb5b519d-c67d-5a80-8e09-395571ae29b1.short_description: Nearly square textile with fringed ribbon and all-over silver and gold embroidery. In the middle appears a *tughra*, the monogram of the Ottoman sultans. The composition of the design with a smaller inner and a larger outer circle suggests the textile was used as a turban cover.
eb5b519d-c67d-5a80-8e09-395571ae29b1.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
eb5b519d-c67d-5a80-8e09-395571ae29b1.method_for_datation: The textile shows the influence of European rococo in design, which increased on urban embroidery at the beginning of the 13th / 19th century. The *tughra* in this embroidery, although simplified and distorted, might be that of Sultan 'Abd al-'Aziz ((r. 1277–93 / 1861–76). However, one should note that all *tughras* of the sultans in the 13th / 19th century show similar features.
eb5b519d-c67d-5a80-8e09-395571ae29b1.method_for_provenance: The design and the *tughra* show that it is a Turkish embroidery. Embroideries of the professional workshops of Istanbul and Bursa were of high technical quality as seen in this fabric. Their patterns are characterised by fine gradation in colour and influenced by European rococo.
