ee26487e-5cf4-5952-b08b-0f2364696f96.name: Ottoman pillow cover
ee26487e-5cf4-5952-b08b-0f2364696f96.short_description: Bursa, located to the south of Istanbul, was the centre of silk velvet weaving from the 15th to the 17th century. Locally produced silk velvet textiles stitched with gold and silver threads were also popular in Europe. When the Austrian Commercial Museum mounted the first international exhibition of oriental carpets in 1891, historic silk velvet brocades from Bursa were amongst the most important objects displayed. Wealthy Ottomans had a particular liking for pillow covers (*yastık*) of silk velour (*çatma*). This Ottoman pillow cover shows cartouches with alternating inverted Persian lettering: *mobarak bad* (good luck), *sa‘adat bad* (prosperity).

f0ec39f8-905e-5c73-87ea-5225163d384d.short_description: The simple red cotton plain weave exterior of this tent contrasts with the dramatic and elaborate embroidered decoration of the interior, probably accomplished in the Iranian town of Resht, a locale famous for its rich embroidery in chain-stitch technique. The tent comprises four walls, with a door panel at the end of one long side, and a gabled top made from two large rectangular panels and two triangular pediments, one at each end. The interior features appliquéd red, blue, green, and yellow pieced wool plain-weave fabrics embellished with tambour chain-stitch embroidery (the so-called *rashi* technique). Leather has been added to reinforce points of potential stress, wear, and friction.

f0fbf3fe-1168-5514-90da-4ae1a4c94a50.name: Brocade.
f0fbf3fe-1168-5514-90da-4ae1a4c94a50.description:
The aesthetics of this fabric is based on a repetitive design of large medallions and a well-balanced use of only three colours. Finely drawn silver arabesques fill the centre of each medallion, surrounded by a narrow poly-lobed frame of red silk. It follows a row of circles alternately coloured red and silver. A zigzag encloses this inner pattern. Red contoured trefoils and leaves on a golden background form the outer border. A detail which also proves the skill of the designer is the small silver point emphasising the middle of each trefoil.  
This brocade is part of a larger piece formerly used as an antependium (altar frontal). Many of the ecclesiastical textiles made in Sweden include fabrics imported from Persia and Turkey.

fa052673-5ed9-5255-bc4c-8cacacef21c2.name: Kaaba *Kiswah* (Covering)
fa052673-5ed9-5255-bc4c-8cacacef21c2.short_description: Prior to Islam, regional tribes competed to cloak the Kaaba, a religious sanctuary. Every year on the ninth day of the Pilgrimage month, a new *Kiswah* (covering) reveals the Kaaba’s new face in a ceremony while concealing the building’s appearance. Sewn by Egyptian craftsman in 1910, this fragment of the *Kiswah* to the Kaaba in Saudi Arabia represents the curtain covering an architectural door adorned with calligraphy. A generous 220 kilograms of gold and silver embroider the 670 kilograms of black-dyed silk. The year-long manufacture, considered a religious duty, requires precision and laborious processes to create a fitted garment that can withstand the hot sun. Egyptian rural production centres produced the *Kiswah* for centuries. Today, modern media helps witness the production and ritual replacement worldwide with livestream coverage.

fbd001b0-41f7-592f-b717-94dbb55470d2.name: Curtain for the door of the Ka‘ba, with the name of Sultan Abdülmecid ['Abd al-Majid] I
fbd001b0-41f7-592f-b717-94dbb55470d2.short_description:
The curtain for the door of the Ka‘ba – known also as *sitara*, *burda* or *burqu‘* – was by far the most elaborate part of the *kiswa* and was replaced annually. Since Mamluk times, they were made in Egypt, and left Cairo with the *kiswa* accompanied by the caravan of pilgrims amidst great pomp and circumstance.  
  
The design of this curtain is typical of those made at the Dar al-Kiswa in Cairo during the 19th century, and it continued to be used until the early 20th century. Curtains of this type were usually made in four sections which were embroidered and then sewn together, the heavy wire embroidery almost completely obscuring the seams. The silk fabric was backed with heavy canvas which helped support the weight of the wire, which on a heavily embroidered example like this, can weigh anything up to 60 kilograms. With its heavy use of embroidery, this curtain could have easily taken 20 or more embroiderers two months to complete.

ff84f82c-c3c2-50e4-8ddf-d6d4c8fd00cb.name: *Suzani*
ff84f82c-c3c2-50e4-8ddf-d6d4c8fd00cb.short_description: Largely known as ‘Bukhara embroideries’, *suzanis* were much prized in Romania. The term, derived from the Persian *suzan*, which means ‘needle’, is applied to a type of embroideries produced in urban workshops from a region in present-day Uzbekistan. As part of the bride’s dowry *suzanis* vary in size and design, and may serve different purposes. They involve the joint effort of several artisans. At first the composition is drawn on the fabric which is then cut into several pieces in order to be embroidered by other women. Subsequently the embroidered pieces are stitched together; the resulting irregularities add to the particular charm of the ensemble. In spite of obvious stylistic differences between the *suzanis* made in Bukhara, Tashkent, Shahrisabz, or Nurata, a definitive provenance may prove difficult to establish. Irrespective of the manufacturing centre all *suzani* embroideries share a specific chromatic exuberance reminiscent to a certain degree of the Mughal and Ottoman art, and quite unlike the restricted colour range of Central Asian carpets. The present embroidery belongs to the group of so-called ‘large-medallion *suzanis*’, more precisely to an extremely rare subgroup limited until recently to only three other examples. The Persian and Hellenistic motifs treated in a free, unrestrained manner recall the rich cultural heritage of Central Asia, which witnessed the rise and fall of great civilizations.
